speechtext:
Reports indicate that a draft agreement between the United Kingdom and the French Committee of National Liberation relating to the administration of liberated areas of France is now under consideration, and that in view of the joint nature of the operations such an agreement will require the adherence of the United States to become effective. Will the Prime Minister inform the house whether the Canadian government 's being kept fully advised in the matter, and
IMr. Homuth.]
if Canada will be a party to the agreement? Will this matter be one of the subjects of the conversation between the Prime Minister and General Charles de Gaulle on his visit to Ottawa ?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH FRENCH COMMITTEE OF NATIONAL LIBERATION-VISIT OF GENERAL DE GAULLE
speechtext:
In reply to my hon. friend I would say that the government has been kept informed of the conversations that have taken place with respect to the matter to which he has just referred; but it is not expected that Canada will necessarily become a party to any projected agreement.
As hon. members are aware, General de Gaulle will be here to-morrow. I expect to have an opportunity to discuss with him many matters of mutual interest and concern to France and Canada. The subject to which my hon. friend has referred may be one of the questions to be taken up at that time.
While I am speaking of General de Gaulle I may mention that the general is expected to arrive in the city by plane in the morning. Arrangements have been made for a welcome to be extended to him on parliament hill at a quarter after twelve. Seats will be provided for members of parliament in front of the peace tower where General de Gaulle will speak. The General will be the guest of His Excellency the Governor General and Princess Alice at Government house during his stay in the city. The government will give a dinner in honour of General de Gaulle in the evening and on the following day he will be leaving early in the morning for brief visits to Montreal and Quebec. That is the extent of the programme for General de Gaulle's visit to Canada that I am able to give at the moment.

speechtext: Has any investigation been made as to reports of recent disturbances at Peta-wawa camp, and if so, will the Minister of National Defence inform the house as to the cause and nature of the disturbances and -the steps which are being taken to ensure that there will be no recurrence?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence):
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: DISTURBANCES AT PETAWAWA CAMP
speechtext:
I have had telephone inquiries
made, and the information which I have with regard to one training centre-there are two- is that at this centre, presided over by Colonel Johnston, the only disturbance in recent days took place two weeks ago in the neighbourhood of the canteen, when two general servicemen got into an altercation with regard to a speech which has had a good deal of publicity in the newspapers. The soldiers were separated before a fight actually took place. The officer commanding the training centre also says positively this is the only disturbance that he knows of in this camp or in his training centre for a considerable time past.
The other training centre is A-2. I have not the name of the commanding officer. An incident occurred there about two months ago in which there was a rumour that -there was a fight between a N.R.M.A. soldier and a general serviceman. Inquiry was made and it was found out that altercation did start in the canteen, but it was immediately stopped and there was no further disturbance. There were only two men involved in each case.
Inquiry from the chief of police of Pembroke shows that there has been no fighting by soldiers in the town of Pembroke for the last three months. The troops have been well-behaved. Brigadier Thackeray, who is in command of Petawawa camp, states that there was no necessity to use a fire hose, as reported in the newspapers, to quell a disturbance because there have been no disturbances.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed from Thursday, July 6, consideration of the motion of Hon. J. L. Usley (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and. means, and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Rowe.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not going to take the time of the house this afternoon in discussing the financial provisions of the budget which were so convincingly set out by my colleague the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) with the clarity and forcefulness which are characteristic of every presentation he makes to this house. Neither am I going to discuss the financial clauses of the amendment provided by the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe). I want to get down to the clause in the amendment which deals with man-power. What I want to do, first, is to tell the house what purposes the N.R.M.A.
The Budget-Mr. Ralston

personnel in this country are serving; secondly, what I can about the situation with regard to reinforcements, and, thirdly, our reasons for recruiting.
In the first place I want to say this, that there is no formation or organization in Canada known as the home defence army. What is referred to are men in the Canadian Army to-day who have been called up for service in Canada. Those men are not in any one formation or organization. They are scattered throughout the ranks of the Canadian Army in Canada, and in practically every branch of that army.
There seems to be an idea that the seventy odd thousand men referred to in the amendment are hived somewhere, or that they are sitting around doing nothing. That is quite untrue, as I think I shall show. The N.R.M.A. personnel, that is the personnel called up under the National Resources Mobilization Act, consists at the present time of something like 73,000. There were 144.000 of them enrolled altogether; in other words, 70,000 of them have gone active or been discharged. Most of those could not measure up to the army medical standards for overseas, and they have been released for civilian work.
I should like hon. members for a moment or two to look into just what these individuals are doing. Here is a break-down with respect to those 73,000 men. About 35,000 of them are on operational duties. About 13,000 of them are on non-operational duties. About
14.000	of them are in training centres. About
4.000	are in depots-wings which have to do with appraisal and placement and rehabilitation. Over 7,000 are on leave,' or are on assigned duty, doing civilian work. That makes up the 73,000.
There are only three of those classes to which one has to pay much attention so far as describing their duties is concerned. First there are those engaged in operational duties, numbering, as I said, about 35,000. Then come those engaged in non-operational duties, to the number of 13,000, and the 14,000 in training centres. The men in depots, it will be understood, are there for purposes of replacement and reappraisement as to their suitability for jobs, and are posted as jobs come up.
Mr. GRAYDON; In connection with the
14.000	in training centres, I take it that those men are undergoing training now. Am I correct in that?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, that is correct. Then, the 7,000 on leave or on assigned duty require no explanation. I wish hon. members to bear in mind that figure when the discussion comes

up from time to time as to what the army is doing in respect of supplying man-power for civilian purposes.
I shall not have time this afternoon to deal with every aspect of the matter I should like to deal with, but I should like just to underline here the fact that something like 7,000 of these N.R.M.A. men are to-day on leave doing civilian jobs-and about 4,000 of general service personnel in addition.
The operational units are scattered from Prince Rupert to Jamaica. They are on the Pacific coast in about a dozen positions, and on the Atlantic coast in about 15 different locations. They are in Newfoundland, in Labrador, at Nassau, Bermuda and Jamaica. In addition to that, a body of these operational troops are doing anti-sabotage duty in the interior of this country. They are engaged also in coast artillery work, signals, anti-aircraft, searchlights, engineers, infantry- they are in almost every branch of the army which provides supply, equipment and other services for operational troops.
There are in addition some in special training at the present time for certain types of operation in which they might be required. That number is included in this 35,000, and would equal about two brigade groups or a little more than that. These operational troops I have mentioned are in locations extending from Prince Rupert to Jamaica. So far as the Pacific and Atlantic coasts particularly were concerned, these operational troops were disposed after consultation with our friends in the United States in connection with the joint defence plan. Hon. members will recall that back in 1942, after Pearl Harbor, insistent demands were made for more troops. At that time the sixth, seventh and eighth divisions were authorized, and immediately all these men were called up. Kiska came in August of 1943. Immediately after Kiska the army disbanded two of those divisions, namely the seventh and eighth. There was a good deal of furore at the time; people thought we were going out of the war. What we thought we were doing was something which was extremely desirable and proper-that is, to release men, if we could, to civilian life. N.R.M.A. men physically unfit for overseas service who were not required for service in Canada were discharged. Other N.R.MA. men not fit for overseas service were posted to replace and release for overseas service general service men who were physically fit for that service. The N.R.M.A. men physically fit for overseas service and who were released by the disbandment were trained as potential reinforcements for overseas service. That was in August, 1943.

The Budget-Mr. Ralston
Somebody asks: Well, what about this matter of defence, anyway? I wish to say this frankly, that since the invasion of a few weeks ago the situation has changed considerably. We had maintained a very limited number of these operational troops on the two coasts- limited, I mean, in the sense that there were a large number of posts they had to look after, and therefore the numbers in any one location were comparatively small. In Labrador and Newfoundland they formed local reserves, and were on aerodrome defence and) anti-aircraft defence. We had to employ these troops according to the needs of defence as determined by what we call the probable scales of .attack which were laid down by the staffs of the United States and Canada. Those scales of attack mean this, that those who know about these matters, staffs w'ho are familiar with the strategic situation, appraise the possibilities and come to the conclusion as to what likely form of enemy attack might be practicable, what form of attack might be expected, and what the nature and extent of that attack might be. They consider also where such attack might possibly come. Troops are then disposed and posted, having those possible scales of enemy attack in view. Hon. members will understand that. On the two coastlines of Canada the troops have been located in bodies of appropriate size at strategic points. I recall that less than a year ago-about the year's end-there was an alarm -in fact one on the Atlantic coast and one on the Pacific coast. I can well imagine what would have been the criticism levelled at the Department of National Defence had there .not been some troops to stand to at that time. Nevertheless the situation, as I say, has changed. At the present time there is under discussion the question of the necessity for operational troops at certain points with a view to a further reduction.
Now, with regard to anti-sabotage. There is a considerable body of troops being used in connection with a particular installation in Canada, and those troops are now disposed in the guarding of that particular development. So much for the 35,000 N.R.M.A. men in operational troops-and1 that is about half of the 73,000 men to whom reference has been made so often and who have been referred to in the amendment.
I now come to non-operational troops, numbering, as I have said, some 13,000. These are troops on training centre staffs, training school staffs, training organization staffs, and personnel employed as administrative personnel, firemen, general duty personnel, clerks, drivers, mechanics and cooks. These men are engaged in service of the establishments of the Canadian Army in Canada, and those establishments, in turn, form the base for equipment and reinforcement for our Canadian Army overseas.
These men are employed with the R.C. E.M.E., which is the corps of electrical and mechanical engineers which has, among other things, to do with the maintenance of vehicles. Perhaps when I tell the house that something like 20,000 to 30,000 vehicles have to be maintained and serviced, hon. members will realize why it takes a considerable number of men to do this work. These men are employed at the establishments in Canada which not only services the equipment produced in Canadian factories for Canada but also provides for the crating and the preparing for shipment of all equipment which goes to the united nations from our productive industries. The house might be interested in knowing that in this particular establishment there are over 150 carloads inward and 150 carloads outward practically every day. These N.R.M.A.. men are employed in large numbers there.
Ordnance handles everything for the army except food and medical stores, and these men are employed at ordnance depots and establishments at headquarters and across the country in large numbers. N.R.M.A. personnel work at the London central mechanization depot and they work at certain special experimental establishments.
In the army service corps N.R.M.A. personnel are employed as drivers, general duty men, supply depot personnel, butchers, bakers and cooks. They are employed also in hospitals and other medical units as well as in headquarters and servicing units where they work in the pay corps, postal corps, corps of military staff clerks and as general duty personnel.
All these men are part of the personnel used to service the army both in Canada and overseas. The big bulk of N.R.M.A. men among the non-operational personnel are for servicing duties, for which general service personnel would otherwise be required. I should also say that the N.R.M.A. personnel help to make up the army service corps detachments which service the navy and air force. They are employed also in woodcutting detachments and in port companies.
Next come the 14,000 N.R.M.A. in the training stream, at training centres, schools and other establishments. These men when trained are used to replace and release general service personnel; to replace N.R.M.A. personnel not medically fit for overseas and they are also a potential pool for reinforcements for overseas if the need should arise.
465ti
The Budget-Mr. Ralston

I have already spoken of the 4,000 odd N.R.M.A. men in the depots to which they are allocated or where they are reassigned to jobs for which they may be fitted.
I have also spoken of the 7,000 on leave or on assigned duties. This would cover men on compassionate leave, compassionate farm leave, industrial leave, lumbering leave, forestry leave, coal mining leave, spring leave and other leave.
That is the home defence army so-called. It is made up of personnel who are serving, as I said, not only from one side of this continent to the other but from the Pacific ocean down into the Caribbean. Except those who are on leave or in depots, all these men are on posts or in training. Quite a few of them are enlisting for general service and in due time will go overseas if they are of a suitable age and category and are fit. So that we have these men, equal in numbers to two brigade groups, who are in the training centres and who if the emergency should arise and the necessary action were taken could be made available promptly to be sent as reinforcements. That would be subject, of course, to the fact that the men in the training centres would have to complete their training.
You say to me, "What will happen if this home defence army in Canada is reduced, if the operational troops in Canada are reduced?" My policy will be to discharge, first, those who are unfit for overseas service to the extent that they can be spared. There will probably not be many who can be spared. They will be used to release for training N.R.M.A. men who are fit for service overseas. Our policy will be to use men fit for overseas service to make up a smaller number of operational units. These units would be composed of men fit for overseas service to the greatest extent possible. Fit men who are made available because of the reduced establishment in operational units in Canada would also go into training units in order that they might be trained for whatever service might be necessary. N.R.M.A. men unfit for overseas would also be used to replace general service men in order to release them for overseas.
I suggest that the statement which I have given regarding the activities of the N.R.M.A. personnel rather destroys the foundation for the regret which was registered by the amendment moved by the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe. We have to have men in Canada, not only to perform defence duties and for internal security, but to provide the service necessary for training and equipping the men in our overseas army. We can no more disband these troops wholesale than can the navy or the air force disband the establishments which they have in Canada and which are
#!
necessary to the valiant service being rendered by our sailors and airmen on every battle front. There are large numbers in all three services, even of those who have volunteered but who will not be able to gratify their ambition to go overseas because they are necessary in Canada. I repeat that we shall if possible reduce considerably the number of operational troops, but those who are fit and can be released from operational duties will be put in training to be ready for any emergency.
The hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe talked about disbanding these N.R.M.A. men and sending them back to the farm and industry. May I say to him that I have no idea of disbanding or discharging physically fit men from the Canadian army, either N.R.M.A. men or general service personnel, while our men overseas are engaged in the greatest conflict of all time, and so long as these men or some of them may be needed as reinforcements. Their training and fitness for service must be kept up.
I do not want the house to think that if the whole 73,000 of the N.R.MA. personnel were sent to England instead of being kept in Canada, that would end the call-up or end recruiting. I am determined to provide for every emergency if I can, and until someone who knows can guarantee to me that it is not necessary any longer, I will keep on recruiting and calling up men in order to have a backlog over here of trained and fit men if an emergency should come.
I want to make this further point in connection with the demand that is always made on the army for men for civilian work. I do not think the people of Canada or the members of this house realize how many men the army has discharged to civilian work. During the last six months we have discharged nearly 5,000 a month, or a total of 30,000 men, of whom about 7,000 were N.R.M.A. personnel. These men have gone back into the civilian manpower pool. While not physically fit for the army they can be utilized in large measure for civilian work. I want to say that the army is not holding on to any men it can spare who are not medically fit for service overseas.
There is another service which the army performs, and I think my colleague the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) will agree with me in this. By the call-up the army is providing an opportunity to check the man-power of this country and to divert and direct them into suitable channels. The army rejects nearly fifty per cent of the men who present themselves for enlistment or for enrolment under the N.R.M.A., and so far as the N.R.M.A. personnel are concerned those men

The Budget-Mr. Ralston
are rechecked by the national selective service officers who may direct them to suitable employment, This means that the army call-up has brought out thousands of men and made them available for more useful and essential work.
So much for the N.R.M.A. personnel. The statement I have just made is not one that is made for the first time. The hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe could have looked up the record in Hansard for the early days of the session and he would have found that I had made almost the same elaboration of the duties being performed by these men. But he just elects in his amendment to assume that these men are doing nothing and that they may be at any moment moved out of the Canadian army organization in Canada and either sent back to the farming industry or moved overseas. I submit that that picture is far from being a true one.
With regard to the matter of reinforcements, an attempt has been made to regard the call for recruits in this country as evidence of an immediate need of reinforcements. The talk had been as if the recruiting activities were because of that need. But I would point out-and it seems to me that it does not take much imagination to realize it without having it specifically pointed out-that recruiting is not for the purpose of providing immediate reinforcements. Recruiting would be no good to provide immediate reinforcements. Men have to be trained for reinforcement purposes for at least six months; and recruiting is for the purpose of replenishing and keeping up our flow of reinforcements six months from now. What we are doing from day to day is to get these men in and train them.
Now, with regard to the matter of reinforcements, I have spoken of this many times, but I am afraid I have not yet made it plain; apparently there is an idea that the only way we can replace casualties is by dispatching men direct from Canada. That is not so. On the contrary, we have overseas a large reinforcement pool, and that pool is calculated on a scale to provide reinforcements for a certain number of months of intense operations. As I have told the house repeatedly, the size of that pool is based on requirements which are calculated from experience and from the best forecast which can be made of casualties. The pool was formed so that we would have reinforcements ready without being dependent on immediate dispatches from Canada. That pool enabled us to make good in a matter of days the losses suffered in the opening phases of the invasion. Already
I have reports of the satisfaction of the commanders in the field, both in Italy and in France, with the efficient way in which reinforcements have been handled.
This is the position of the pool. My officers advise me that our reinforcement situation overseas at the end of June on an over-all basis was better than called for in our plans. That is on an over-all basis. But as I have said before, it is very difficult always to match supply with requirements in every trade and in every arm, in view of the inevitable variation in requirements. Any one of these trades or arms may receive a sudden demand when the others may remain for the time being almost untouched. The pattern of war changes constantly; and the responsible officers are continually comparing actual conditions with those forecast and are taking prompt action, by retraining and reallocation, to adjust for any situation which may be out of line with previous estimates. My advice is that subject to those adjustments between arms and trades the pool overseas was at the end of June at an adequate level for its purpose, and that is after allowing for casualties up to that date.
It must be understood that the reinforcement pool will not remain always at the same strength. It goes down and up, like a city reservoir which is drawn on heavily when a fire occurs and which rises gradually during normal times. There will no doubt be times ahead when the pool will be lowered very considerably, as casualties occur. It will be gradually raised later by monthly dispatches. 1 add this, that we are not counting in that pool those in hospital, no matter how soon they may be available-I do not mean only the wounded, but those temporarily or otherwise sick, so long as they are in hospital- or those attending courses in the United Kingdom. All those we class for the time being as non-effectives.
What are we going to do for the men to send over monthly-these monthly dispatches I have spoken of? The hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) said, "Where are these men to come from if not from this immobilized force, Canada's home army?" Well, I will try to tell him. We anticipate that from the general service men we actually have in hand at the present time we shall be able for some months to come to dispatch month by month the quotas of reinforcements we have planned for. I do not want to be overoptimistic, but I would say that we have in hand at the present time sufficient general service men to complete our quotas right up to the calendar year end.
The Budget-Mr. Ralston

Where do we get these men to dispatch? I am not talking about men enlisting, I am talking about men we actually ha-ve in hand. Well, we have general service personnel in training centres all over Canada, and we have general service men in operational and nonoperational units who are being made available as reinforcements by orderly withdrawal and replacement and, in some cases, retraining. I said in February that we had about sixty thousand of these. The number now stands at probably fifty thousand or better. Then, as I said in February, we have in addition about fifty thousand of these N.R.M.A. personnel of whom I spoke a little while ago, who would be of suitable age and category to be drawn on for overseas service if the necessity should arise and appropriate action were taken under N.R.MA. As I have indicated, those in the brigade groups who are fit could be sent quickly, and how many of the others could be sent would depend on the comparative need. Of course we must go short in Canada if the need is over there.
I have already stressed that the army in Canada has the task of servicing, equipping and reinforcing of the army overseas. That is the situation. But we cannot stop there. The war is not over. As I have said repeatedly, Hitler and Tojo are not licked. There will be big battles yet, and Canada will be in the thick of them. That brings me to this matter of activity about recruiting. People may ask, "Why all this activity? Why do we not stand on what we haye?" The answer is that we want to protect the position six months from now, and I am not content to rely on protecting that position by using draftees if we can reinforce our army with volunteers. Our recruiting activities are for the purpose of keeping up enlistments from now on so as to be able to maintain the stream of reinforcements from month to month. We want to get, if we can, an average of 4,000 a month or better from those not now in the army, and that figure may have to be reviewed, depending on the developments of the present operations.
From January to May inclusive the average number volunteering for general service was just about 3,800 general service men a month. Included in that average is about 600 N.R.M.A. personnel who enlisted for general service.
For June, according to the daily returns we have, the number volunteering will be over 6,000, and that includes between 2,500 and 3,000 N.R.MA. personnel who have enlisted for general service. I pause to ask if that is not a better way to utilize these N.R.MA. men for reinforcements. I know from reports I have received that enlisting gives them a new outlook, new self-respect, a determination that

comes from having made a great decision. And all that is bound to make them better soldiers.
Some of these former N.R.MA. men would have to be retrained in another arm of the service, but many of them are ready now for overseas service. But the civilians who are enlisting-who are just coming into the army for the first time-all have to be trained, and that takes six months at least if they are to get all the training we should like. That means that a man enlisting to-day from civilian life and put into training would not, in all probability, come out at the other end of the training stream and be ready to go overseas at the earliest before the 1st of January, 1945. So that the short answer to the question "Why are we recruiting,?" is that we are recruiting so that the flow of reinforcements six months from now will keep right on.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
May I ask the minister
whether there has been any reduction in the length of training given to general service personnel in Canada?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: None that I know of.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Is it intended that there
shall be a reduction?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Not that I know of.
As I told the house in February, if current recruiting did not keep up, our quotas for dispatch overseas in the closing months of this year and in the first months of the new year would be down, and that would mean that if casualties occurred on the scale we calculated for, the pool overseas would be lowering instead of filling up. In that connection the house will be glad to know that from the very beginning of the campaign in the Mediterranean, all through Sicily and Italy, and in the Normandy invasion, the casualties, while substantial, have thus far been considerably below those for which we estimated. We devoutly hope that may continue, but we certainly must not bank on it. And so, I say, we are keeping right on now getting men to enlist for overseas service, and from what I have said you will see that there are two sources from which these enlistments can come-the N.R.M.A. men now in the arm}q and men enlisting from civilian life. We are placing before both these groups the needs overseas and asking them to join the army of volunteer soldiers which has distinguished itself in every operation in which it has taken part.
As I speak I am reminded that to-day is the anniversary of the invasion of Sicily. I am sure it is a red letter day in the history of the Canadian Army-a day on which

The Budget-Mr. Ralston
Canadians will look back with pride and thankfulness as they recall the exploits of that landing at Pachino and of the thirty-nine days following it, during which Sicily was [DOT] liberated.
There they made their place in the renowned Eighth Army. The reputation for soldiering which they won in Sicily was carried forward by the 1st Division and the Army Tank Brigade as abreast the British formation they spearheaded the landing on the toe of Italy at Reggio Calabria. Steadily and irresistibly they fought their way northward. Later they were joined by an Armoured Division, with which they formed the 1st Canadian Corps. The battles of Ortona and the Liri valley, the breaching of the Gustav and Adolf Hitler lines, were a few of the outstanding achievements which have written their names in shining letters on the pages of Canadian history.
For a long while the Canadian army was not in active operation. Young men went into the navy and the air force, many of them because they thought they could get into action sooner. The army to-day challenges any man who wants action and who wishes to help to finish the war and finish it quickly.
I have spoken of the sources of enlistments. These are the sources from which our overseas army is reinforced-the pool which is now overseas; the pool of general service men in Canada; the N.R.M.A. men now in the army who are enlisting because they see their duty; and young men in civilian life who cannot pick up a newspaper or listen to the radio without realizing that the call is to them. In addition, there are the drafted N.R.M.A. men who are potential overseas reinforcements if the need for sending them should arise and the necessary action is taken. About them and others who may be called up, I have made my position clear more than once in the house. That position is this-I am for keeping our army overseas 100 per cent volunteers if we can do it; but if we cannot maintain the army overseas with volunteers and it is necessary to send N.R.M.A. men, there can be no alternative for me but to recommend action under the act, and I shall do so. I simply want to point out that nearly two and a half years ago, when this same question was up in the house, I said:
I have faith in the success of the voluntary method if we all do our part. With the background and traditions which this country possesses, and which it would be folly to ignore,
I prefer the voluntary method if it works, and I shall do all I can to make it work.
That was in February, 1942. I think I can say that I have faithfully tried to raise and administer the Canadian army under the
voluntary system. Since that time when I spoke, 198,000 men have enlisted voluntarily in the army. That is an average of over 6,600 per month since February, 1942. The total voluntary enlistment in the three services in Canada since the time I spoke was 378,000 men. Those figures would seem to show that my faith in the voluntary system was justified then. I intend to try to see that it does not fail in this last long strong pull.
May I say a word about what I believe is the advantage of recruiting rather than conscripting. I can say to you, Mr. Speaker, that it would be much easier for my officers and myself if we could just by a stroke of the pen draft men for overseas service instead of adjusting, retraining and reorganizing to utilize the general service men, and campaigning for recruits to keep the flow up. But I do not think there is a man in Canada who knows, anything about these things who does not in his heart of hearts believe that where we have an army overseas which is 100 per cent volunteers it will be a better army if we can keep it that way. The men who are there have volunteered from a sense of duty. Is there not bound to be cleavage between them and those who, they feel, are wanting in the spirit of service which has carried them through tough times and enabled them to accomplish the impossible? Comradeship in war means everything and there are some members of the house who know that: the dependence of one man on the other, the confidence and friendship which grow up between men who have made the same great decision and who-fight each for the other. Men in that position have a sure knowledge that the man on the right or the left will not let the show down. That is esprit de corps, and it is one of the most vital things in battle. The operations of this war have been in fast, hard-hitting movement. Men in small groups scattered over a wide territory have had to be on their own. Canadian resourcefulness and initiative, born of a sense of duty, have made fighting men, with confidence in each other as members of a team, able to hold on and drive forward to overcome obstacles and rout the enemy in situations where nothing but loyalty to the cause could have succeeded. I think it almost goes without saying that any soldier on a dangerous task would prefer to have as comrades those who, like himself, had volunteered to serve.
I know that other countries have drafted armies. That is true of the United States, of Britain and of New Zealand, and I know the magnificent way they have fought. But their system of draft was in force practically from the very beginning. The men in the forces: are all on an equal level there, and the draft
The Budget-Mr. Ralston

was simply to decide who should go first and who would be best suited to go. In the early days in some of those countries a man could volunteer, but no stigma attached to a man because he was drafted; it simply indicated to the man that it was his turn. For better or for worse, that was not our system; it was agreed by both major parties in 1940 that it would not be. It is not the system in Australia. In Australia men who are called up can only be sent as far north as the equator, and Australia's contribution to the war has many times, and rightly so, been held up in this house as one that we should emulate. It is not the system in South Africa, where the only power to call men up for compulsory service is for service within the union itself. And South Africa has as her Prime Minister Field Marshal Smuts, whose war-mindedness has been worthily applauded throughout the commonwealth.
And so to sum up, Mr. Speaker. My job is to maintain our army overseas. My job is to do all I can to see that Canada backs to the limit her men who are overseas. If the sending of these N.R.M.A. men is necessary to maintain the army overseas at the present time, then I shall be for sending them. If it is necessary for that purpose at any time in the future, I shall be for sending them. But so long as volunteers enlist for that purpose, does anyone doubt that we would serve those soldiers overseas better by sending them volunteers like themselves instead of draftees?
And now if I may I wish just for a minute to step into' the sphere of my colleague the Minister of Finance. I have referred to this before, but there is an analogy that people sometimes miss, and I am speaking now particularly with regard to the help which citizens can give in connection with recruiting as compared with the help they give in connection with war loans. My colleague the Minister of Finance has to raise huge amounts of money every year to pay for war activities. Only about half of it is raised by compulsion, that is, by taxes. The government, under the very act, the National Resources Mobilization Act, which authorizes the sending of men by compulsion, has the power to force citizens to- give their money and their property for the prosecution of the war. Why nht take it all by compulsion? But my colleague with the full approval of the Canadian people does not take it that easy way. On the contrary, he puts a vast amount of time, energy and money into recruiting campaigns for dollars-to persuade and urge the people of Canada to contribute their money by buying victory bonds. More than that, through the national war finance
	i/JHl
committee, he asks and receives the patriotic support of thousands of citizens to make those campaigns successful. The campaigns are . strenuous. Competition is stimulated between communities, plants and organizations. Badges, emblems and shields are prepared to recognize those who respond and to spur on those who do not. I commend that to some critics who suggested we should not give the general serviceman a GS. badge to wear. Honeyed words do not always produce results. Sometimes people have to have their duty pointed out to them pretty forcibly. Great people, famous people and popular people are brought in to help to influence citizens to subscribe. When it is all over, we Canadians are proud, and rightly so, that success has been achieved by many methods in bringing home to people their duty and their privilege.
Is it so very different regarding furnishing the needs of war for men instead1 of dollars? We use compulsion to get men for service in Canada. We have the power to use compulsion for service overseas. But we have not done it. We have taken the harder way deliberately, and so far it has been successful. We have voluntarily enlisted in the armed services altogether something like, I think,
800,000	men and women. If it is righteous and patriotic and laudable to support our men overseas by asking our neighbours to contribute money by buying bonds instead of having it taken by force, is it not just as patriotic and laudable when it comes to supporting those same men by influencing the young men of Canada to go as reinforcements rather than regarding it as none of our business and saying, let the government force them to go? The great advantage, Mr. Speaker, in getting the voluntary cooperation of citizens in raising money or in raising men is that it puts people's hearts into the war. Therefore I believe that my officers and I, and Canadians generally, can best do our duty to our army in the field by working just as hard and loyally and ceaselessly to recruit men as we do to recruit dollars.
Right here I want to express the hearty thanks, not only of myself and of the government and of the department, but of the people of Canada and the troops overseas, to the officers and staffs at headquarters and in the commands and districts, and to citizens' committees and individual citizens all over this country, for their hard, loyal and unflagging work to provide volunteer reinforcements for our volunteer army overseas. The task is not an easy one. There are two classes in this country who do make it difficult. One class consists of those who are insistent on conscrip-

The Budget-Mr. Matthews
tion whether we can get volunteers or not. Consciously or unconsciously, they discourage volunteer recruiting by .constantly keeping up the agitation, criticizing and disparaging the efforts of those who are loyally giving their best efforts to persuade and urge young men of Canada to enlist. The other class is a group that is against overseas service and who protest against conscription but do nothing to avoid it by encouraging our men to volunteer. In connection with the groups I have mentioned I hope most sincerely that the attitude may change. Perhaps nothing that I have said may change it, but I would hope it might because I do think that there is a sound basis of common sense, patriotism and efficiency in having and maintaining our army a volunteer army at this time.
But there is another group, and that is the group of people who do not speak in public and who do not write in the newspapers. They are people who think and work faithfully and quietly. They know that Canada has done and is doing a grand job in the war. I say "Canada" deliberately, for it is the Canadian people who have given of time, effort and money, and more than all, the dearest possessions of young men and young women from their homes. They do not see the point of raising this explosive issue at this crucial time in a war like this. They can wait to express their views on the government's conduct of the war when the time comes. They are not of the class which says Canada has done too much. They may think that conscription may perhaps be fairer in theory, but they know that the will to serve is better in practice. They are not so much interested in methods as in results. For them the winning of the war comes first. That group of quiet, thinking citizens of this country has given its support to the war all through those years. I ask them, and I wish to ask all true Canadians, no matter of what race or sect, or what province or party, to show the pride which I know they have in the magnificent achievements of our men in Italy, Sicily and Normandy by helping us to continue to send them the very best we have.

speechtext: May I ask the minister a question? Has not the Australian government this year abrogated the limiting clause on the Australian militia?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not that I know of.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Following the very inspiring address we have just heard I intend to make any remarks of mine very brief. Since this budget discussion has been prolonged there are only a few points to which I desire to refer. First of all I want
to join with many other hon. members in extending my sincere congratulations to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) upon the able budget speech that he delivered to this house. I have come to regard the minister as the mystery man of Canada. It is true that he does not resort to the pulling of rabbits from the hat, but he extracts from the pockets and the persons of the Canadian people bank dollars and cheques with a deftness of approach that prompts them to invite him to come again, and come again he will. It is true that the people do a certain amount of complaining regarding the paying of taxes, but I venture to say that not in all Canada is there a man who to any greater extent, if as great, commands the respect, the esteem and confidence of the Canadian people as does the Minister of Finance.
I do not intend to take up the time of the house in a discussion of monetary theories. We have heard a great deal of them, but any reading I have done along that line has forced me to the conclusion that in the realm of finance, as in any other realm, we cannot get something for nothing. Any nation or any individual who has proceeded along that line has in the end met with disappointment and generally near disaster.
I have before me three statements which I shall not take the time to quote. They come presumably from authoritative sources and refer to the national debt of Canada. Strangely enough, they all differ as regards the amount, but they are unanimous in pointing us to the conclusion that our debt has reached-and is going still farther-staggering and appalling figures. One statement gives the gross unmatured funded debt as $10,689,000,000 on March 31, 1944. Other amounts would have to be added as well. It does not give me a great deal of comfort to be told that this debt is owing in Canada. It is debt just the same, no matter where it is owing. Nor is it any comfort to know that only sixty per cent of the wage earners of Canada are contributing to the investment in that debt, so that the debt itself is not payable to the people of Canada but only to a portion of the people.
I am not referring to these matters in any spirit of criticism, and I do not want to be so understood. I am referring to them for the reason that I believe the time has come when every man, woman and child in Canada should support the finance minister of to-day or of to-morrow in his efforts to curtail unnecessary expenditure wherever possible. In the past the people of Canada have not complained about the debt. They are not going to complain in the future as long as they feel that their money is not wasted. We have had no alternative. All down through the years since

The Budget-Mr. Matthews

o'clock, night after night, month after month, and I ride on a Bank street car. Almost every night I see in that car perhaps a dozen or two dozen soldiers and airmen. Time and again I have noted the gentlemanly bearing of these men, and I have wished on many occasions that their parents could be with me in that car to see for themselves the manly conduct of their sons in uniform-their sons who are fighting in freedom's cause. I put this on record as a tribute, and perhaps also as a comfort to the mothers and fathers across Canada who suffer heartache and suspense in these days. Could they see their boys here in Ottawa, and in other cities I have visited, they would not feel any great uneasiness about them. I take this opportuntiy to pay a sincere tribute to the fine character of the enlisted boys of Canada.
Mrs. DORISE W. NIELSEN (North Battleford): Mr. Speaker, this budget has already been widely discussed, and some very divergent points of view have been expressed. By far the greater part of the criticism thus far has been respecting the financial undertakings of the government. To many members the budget appears to be somewhat of an abstract document, dealing as it does with such tremendous sums of money-sums beyond the comprehension of most ordinary people. Some of the speeches made by hon. members, such as the one made by the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Jackman), are obviously intended to impress the house with the members' knowledge of fiscal policies and so on. However, to me the budget still remains a human document. I feel that it is not such an abstract thing as some people might imagine it to be.
In looking through the minister's speech as recorded in Hansard it seems to be a living document expressing the life and the lifeblood of the nation. It is a word picture of our people, of their problems from day to day. It expresses in no uncertain terms both the heights and the depths of their achievements and their possibilities. It expresses also their assets and liabilities, their dreams and failures, their hopes and defeats. The highlights of the budget of course are seen in the vast volume of production that has rolled from our mines, our forests, our farms, our shops and mills, wherever the labour of our men and women has been applied to the natural resources of this great country. That results naturally in the height of the national income which has been achieved.
I felt it was a good thing that the government tiad nut considered only the financial war effort. As our allied armies have pressed forward the government undoubtedly has

thought of much longer term problems and has presented them in this budget. It dealt with such things as getting rid of restrictions imposed by the War Exchange Conservation Act, and there was also the repeal of customs duties and the war exchange tax on agricultural implements. All of these endeavour in some degree to better the conditions of our people. With regard to the changes made in connection with agricultural implements I shall have more to say a little later.
It is evident also that the government has given much thought to the two great groups within Canada, business and labour, on this question of taxation. I have no doubt that the outstanding problem presented to the government on behalf of business was the lack of sufficient liquid funds for the conversion of industry to peace-time production. I am perfectly certain in my own mind that their problem is not as great as it was represented to be. The government has been more than generous in what it has done to recognize their problem and to make allowance for it.
There have been widespread protests from the labour movements in the past which make it clear that the taxation policy of this government has * not been satisfactory and has not been endorsed by our labour groups. The tax policy, together with the enforcement of the wage ceiling, has undoubtedly acted1 as a brake upon production. That is not just my statement; it is a statement made by responsible leaders of the trade union movement. To remedy this condition the budget provides for the elimination of the savings portion of- the income tax. Personally I believe that this problem could have been tackled in another way, in a way which would have proved more satisfactory to the labour forces. The workers have always been a little afraid for this refundable portion of the tax and I think something should have been done to allay their fears. It would have been better if the workers could have continued to have a certain portion of their taxes put aside and refunded to them in order that they would have a certain amount in post-war days. But no bond! or certificate was given to the workers to represent this refundable portion of their tax. I believe if the government, had issued a certificate or a small ticket each time a refundable portion of tax was paid the worker would have known quite clearly that the money would be returned. This would have had1 a much more satisfactory effect. Only this last year we have issued $10,200,000 worth of war certificates, which is an indication that the workers are anxious to save whenever it is possible for

The Budget-Mrs. Nielsen
them to do so. By having a certificate they feel quite sure that their savings will be returned) to them.
Another method of handling this problem would have been to remove the tax on overtime pay. This matter has been brought up time after time by the trade unions, and I believe they are justified in saying that the tax on overtime pay has been a bar to and has prevented overtime production which otherwise would have been made. A tax on overtime pay is no incentive to extra production.
As I said before, in my opinion the budget amendments with regard to the refundable portion of the income tax and the taxes on agricultural implements are good, but I am wondering just how they will affect my own people. I am inclined to think fhat the benefits that will accrue to the farming people of North Battleford will not be nearly as great as we thought they might be at first. I find that in 1939 the farming people of Saskatchewan purchased roughly $10,000,000 worth of farm machinery. If we divide that by the twenty-one constituencies in the province we find that each constituency purchased some $482,000 worth. This is not a very close estimate, but it gives a general idea. I believe my constituency would fall below that average, because the great majority of the farms in North Battleford are small farms. When you consider what was spent in 1939 you realize that even with the lowering of the tariff the people in my part of Saskatchewan are not going to benefit greatly in their purchases of farm machinery. Some of them may save a little money on the purchase of machinery, but in my opinion it is quite possible that the money thus saved will have to be used for the payment of income tax. They will be little better off after all. I think it would have been preferable if the government had retained the compulsory savings portion of the tax but had removed the tax completely from the lower brackets. That would have given greater aid to my people.
As I say, to me this budget is a living document because it gives a picture of the inequalities which exist within this country, I do not think anyone will deny that the farm people are receiving a little better income. Our farmers acknowledge themselves that things are a little better. But the undeniable fact remains that as a group our farmers do not yet receive their fair share of the national income. This fact has been stated many times, but it should be reiterated just as long as these inequalities exist. It is your duty, Mr. Speaker, and it is my duty and the duty of all members of this house, to try
to eliminate those inequalities and to see that this group of people, who have contributed so much to the cause of the united nations and to Canada generally, receive a just and fair return.
In my opinion what is needed by way of policy is something which will increase the income of the farming people. That would be the greatest spur to production. It would be an assurance of increased health and wellbeing on the part of the people, and would increase their willingness to share with the rest of the nation the burdens of this war. I do not see how any hon. member can argue that a man should be expected to pay income tax if he is not able to provide adequately for the bodily requirements of himself and his family, and I submit that the present lowest bracket of the income tax does not allow for those decencies of living which this nation should assure its people for their health and well-being. If the minister argues that by the elimination of the refundable portion of the tax inflation will not be increased, it seems to me the same argument applies to the elimination of the tax on the lowest income brackets. In my opinion the lifting of the lowest brackets would have provided more assistance to our people than the elimination of the refundable portion of the tax. Together with higher price guarantees to our farm people, floors underneath farm prices, the definite guarantees of foreign markets, it would have gone far to correct the inequalities of income which still exist among farmers by contrast with those engaged in other industries.
In looking over the ministers' speech of June 26 I notice that, he especially recommended that a commission be set up to inquire into certain matters having to do with fiscal policy. He mentioned particularly the tax on annuities and the matter of succession duties. I wish the minister had gone much farther. In my opinion the reference is not nearly broad enough. We have a tremendous task before us in facing the problems of the transition from war to peace in a changed world. The recommendation to set up a commission is an excellent one, but such a commission should not narrow its activities to such things as the taxation of annuities and succession duties; it should make a complete and comprehensive survey and receive, submissions from all the various groups with regard to their ability to contribute to the national income. Such a commission could study with great advantage -and the inquiry should begin immediately- the whole range of taxation with a view to revising the tax structure to meet the needs of a changing economy. I personally believe that
me
The Budget-Mrs. Nielsen

the tax on personal incomes will and should remain the backbone of any taxation system, but we have to see to it that it is graded far more equitably than at present in accordance with ability to pay.
I have made these few remarks this afternoon with the purpose of looking to the future. On several occasions I have listened to speeches made by members of the C.C.F.; I have in mind particularly a speech made the other evening by the hon. member for York-ton (Mr. Castleden). He spoke of the depression; he enlarged on the difficulties which occurred through the 'thirties; to be quite honest, to me it was a speech ad infinitum, ad nauseam. After all, the hon. member for Yorkton was engaged as a teacher during the depression period; he at least was sure of a living. I could easily occupy not one but many forty-minute periods by talking in this chamber, with far greater knowledge than the hon. member for Yorkton. about, the years of the depression, because I know of these things from personal experience and the experiences of my neighbours. But to what end does anyone to-day get up to speak about the suffering in Canada through the thirties? Why should I add to the story? Already volumes have been written and spoken on the subject. What good can it do to turn our faces to the past? We are living in the year 1944. It seems to me that those who harp upon the difficulties of that bygone period can only destroy the belief of Canadians in their own ability to go forward. We have emerged from the trials of past years, and now the problems of war are with us; but. our faces must be turned towards the future, and any criticisms of the budget or of any government measure should be with a recognition of what that measure can contribute to the future of Canada. In this crucial period of the world's history through which we are passing, those leaders of the C.C.F. who within this house have been contending that unless we have socialism here after the war we must necessarily revert to those terrible times of depression, exhibit an utter inability to understand the changing pattern of the world in which we live.
I am sorry to say these things, but I have to be honest about it; it is far better for me to make these remarks here, where you, Mr. Speaker, and all the world can hear them, than to make assertions at the hustings, as some C.C.F. speakers have done in my part of the country, where it is impossible for anyone to reply. I like to make statements in a place where they can be discussed. I hope
[ Mrs. Nielsen.]
I shall never be guilty of so misleading the people of Canada, or show such immaturity of political thinking; such an utter lack of a scientific approach to the dynamics of social change, as to assert that the only alternative for Canada is socialism or depression. I cannot help saying that such an attitude shows, to my way of thinking, an absolutely infantile analysis of the future which is possible for the Canadian people. To say that these are the only alternatives is to base one's thinking on something which is wishful and utopian; it has no reality, no basis; there is nothing concrete about it. I want definitely to dissociate myself from any who have spoken in such a way.
I have a belief, Mr. Speaker, in the future of Canada and Canada's people. I believe in the ability of Canadians to plan to go forward, to create their own future, as they are quite capable of acting unitedly in this crisis. Statistics show that we are not the nation we were in the hungry thirties. Is there today any hon. member, to whatever political party he belongs, who is not proud of the fact that in the year 1944 Canada, with a population but little over eleven millions, stands first in the production of nickel, of newsprint, of asbestos, of platinum, of radium; second in wood pulp and in gold; third in aluminum, in copper, in zinc, in cobalt, and in silver; fourth in wheat and in lead? As members of parliament we have a tremendous responsibility. We must face the challenge, and assure our people that both after and during the war mutual faith among all classes of our people can and must be substituted in place of suspicion which, too often, characterizes our people in the different provinces. Conditions which cause separation between provinces must be guarded against, and it is my submission that the establishment of equality of privilege with equality of responsibility is an assured way whereby unity can be brought to this nation.
Then, too, all of us must face the challenge that we can assure security with freedom, for unless we reverence freedom and maintain freedom the prospect following the war will be a fearful one. I believe it will be agreed by all that we must not compromise our basic way of life. We must resolutely refuse to sacrifice our freedom in return for a promise of economic security, for history has shown that economic security, without freedom, is meaningless and dangerous to the continuance of our democratic way of life. We in the house have a right and duty to face any infringement or invasion of our rights and freedoms, for if we lose our freedom in the House of Commons, if we lose our inalienable rights as members of parliament, then freedom in this nation will be destroyed.
I do not intend to do anything which would transgress the ruling made by you, sir, the other night, by a discussion of the merits or demerits of 'a speech delivered in another place by Senator Bouchard. But I do say, Mr. Speaker, that when freedom is interfered with in parliament, members of parliament, regardless of political belief, must resist any invasion of their prerogative rights and privileges. Never since 1764 in Great Britain has there been any invasion of the rights of a member of parliament to speak as he feels, to utter words that he believes must be uttered and to carry into effect the noble words of Burke, placed on Hansard in this debate by the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent). Yet the Prime Minister, who so often in the past has spoken of the necessity of upholding the privileges of parliament, has remained silent at the most serious infringement of and challenge to parliame tary free-
The Budget-Mr. Diejenbaker

dom that has taken place anywhere within this empire in a hundred and eighty years. Parliament cannot remain silent.
I have before me the report of the United Kingdom committee on the Sandys case in 1939. Sandys, a son-in-law of Winston Churchill, was alleged to have contravened the provisions of the official secrets act. He was to be called before a military board to give evidence, and a committee of parliament was set up to determine the extent of parliamentary privilege. The report of that committee concludes with these words:
"Parliament without parliamentary liberty," says Pym, "are but a fair and plausible way into bondage. Freedom of debate being once foreclosed the essence of the liberty of parliament is withal dissolved."
I have looked over the records of history disclosing the fight that has taken place over the years waged by members of parliament to assure the maintenance of their right to express themselves as they -would without punishment outside parliament. Those liberties and rights go back a long way. The first example was in the reign of Henry VIII when one Strode was prosecuted for having introduced a bill in the House of Commons. He was fined and imprisoned, but thereupon an act was passed declaring that he was within his rights and could not be punished for exercising his parliamentary rights. Then was established the freedom of a member of parliament to speak without danger of punishment.
Then in 1629, during the days of Hampden, Pym and Eliot, Eliot was prosecuted, and again the right was established that what is spoken in parliament can be judged only in parliament and nowhere else. The principle was redeclared that what is spoken in parliament cannot be dealt with outside parliament. Then, of course, there are the provisions of the Bill of Rights which are declaratory in part of parliamentary privilege. The outstanding and final declaration occurred in 1764 when the king dismissed a general from his position as groom of the bedchamber because he had dared as a member of parliament to speak and vote as he wished. I quote from Anson where it is stated:
The practice was very shortly afterwards discontinued; in fact Burke claims credit to the Rockingham ministry of the following year for having "abolished the dangerous and unconstitutional practice of removing military officers for their votes in parliament."

The Budget-Mr. Pouliot

if he has recourse to such tactics his future is doomed. I advise him honestly and as a friend to use other tactics if he wants to emerge in due course.
For the province of Quebec we have figures given in decimals. Does my hon. friend believe in decimals? Does he believe in the statistics which are supplied by any department? I do not. According to the figures supplied by the bureaucracy Quebec is the goat. Quebec is always the goat. My hon. friend does not know that the figures supplied to members of parliament are prepared by men who do not know how to do the work, whom I had to tell years ago how to do certain work. The hon. member for Vancouver South who was on the civil service committee must remember very well that I had to tell those "experts" how to do certain work, which was badly done. When the chairman of the civil service commission came before us I asked him plainly, "Mr. Bland, is this chart made out as it should be?" He did not answer me. I said, "This item at the right-hand corner, should it not be at the left-hand corner?" He said, "Yes." And so on and so on. Then I called Putman, one of the important members of the civil service commission-I do not know if he is there now-and I had to tell him what to do. I said, "I want this information to-morrow morning." "Oh," he said, "we cannot do it by to-morrow morning." "Then I should like it by to-morrow afternoon." "Oh, sir, please, it is so much work we cannot do it by to-morrow afternoon." "Then I want it done the day after to-morrow by ten o'clock." "Oh, sir, you do not know what it means. It is a tremendous amount of work." Finally I said, "Then I want it by two o'clock the day after to-morrow'. Will you have it, or not?" And then he telephoned me and asked me if it was well done. I had to teach him what to do and how to do it. Without definite instructions from men who know how this work should be done, what guarantee has the hon. gentleman that these figures are correct? What I know and what most hon. members from Quebec know very well is that their counties have been drained, that there are no more men of military age left in our counties. Look at the list of unemployment insurance offices and the selective service offices. No men are applying for positions; no men are available except a few day labourers. On the other hand there are long lists of farmers and men concerned with essential industries who are asking for labour and cannot secure it.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

speechtext:
At six o'clock I had made a reference to the different statements of the national Progressive Conservative chairman McTague on two occasions-on the occasion of his nomination at Guelph and in an interview which was given to the press when he came here to Ottawa. I do not kpow the reason why he has been selected as national chairman. In my humble view, as in the view of many others, that man has been greatly overrated. He is just a man who has been boosted for some reason or another and he is far from being one -who is serious enough to be the national chairman of a great party. I remember the time when the Conservative party was in existence. At that time there was a good man as chairman of the party, a man like the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol), but now that is finished.
There are some observations which I wish to make. I have here a poster which was shown in the windows of large business offices in several cities in Canada and which reads:
Canada's aid to the united nations. The value of eggs, cheese, wheat, flour, canned fish and bacon exported by Canada to members of the united nations in 1943 amounted to:
Eggs	 $ 14,700,000
Cheese	 26,800,000
