subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It looks like an illuminated address.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend the member for Broadview has always a picturesque expression to describe things. Now, sir, we have made a fight for the farmers, certainly not because we are against the war effort. There is a handful of members who have done it, and at the time when the jingoes were tightening the regulations concerning the farmers we made a fight for them in the first instance in connection with the regulations which mentioned agriculture as a seasonal occupation. We succeeded in having that important industry described also as an essential occupation; when the training was extended from one

The Budget-Mr. Pouliot
month to four months we succeeded in having an extension of from four to six months for the farmer, and when the army regulations were changed so that the training was extended from four months to the duration, we succeeded also in having the postponement for farmers extended until further notice. Well, that was something, and the work that was done here by a handful of members who were not afraid to speak their minds helped the constituents of hon. members who are asking so strongly to send men overseas. When I addressed a fine group of men in western Ontario not long ago I said that the farmers of Middlesex county were gaining from the fight waged in parliament by just a handful of Frenchspeaking members, and that is true of the farmers of the whole country. The farmers of Lake Centre and those in the vicinity of Vancouver, the farmers of York-Sunbury, the farmers in the vicinity of Toronto, the farmers of Quebec, the farmers all over the land have been helped by the constant efforts of members of parliament who were not afraid to ask for the exemption of farmers from any military training.
I remember at times we were howled down and called friends of Hitler just because we were thinking of real human values and of the essentiality of these occupations in war time. Opinions are free undoubtedly, but free opinions when they are contradictory cannot all be right, and we were facing all sorts of difficulties, but we were never downhearted and we took the same stand all the time, whether it was the plebiscite or the mobilization bill. On all occasions we waged the fight for the farmers; and those like the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe), who is sponsoring the amendment which is now before the Chair, were always fighting against us as one man. But they did something for the farmer. They said that he should have better prices. That reminds me of something that happened when Mr. Bennett was in power. I said to the chairman one day that I had been passing through his county. It was at the time when unemployment was being discussed so much and I said I had stopped at a certain place to telephone and there was a young lady there. I asked her if she had brothers and she said she had two. I said, "What are they doing?" She said, "One is a qualified carpenter, and he has gone fishing for smelts." I said, "What is the other one doing?" She replied, "He is a mason." I said, "What is he doing now" She replied, "He is hunting ducks." That simply showed that these men who had trades could not find any work. Then, answering certain objections, I said to him, "To whom will you preach
patriotism when all the Canadians are dead of hunger?" And do you know, sir, what happened? The day after, two pages of Hansard were gone; that does not show in Hansard. Instructions were given so that it would not appear in Hansard.
Well, now, I put the same question: Who will farm this country if all the farmers are gone? I have no objection to helping a young man who is willing to go overseas go there, to have all obstacles removed for him if it is his desire. I respect his freedom of choice; but on the other hand if there is a farmer who is essential on the farm he has to be fought for not only with regard to the revenue of farm production but with regard to his stay on the land. Sometimes we are told that we are unpatriotic, that we are bad Canadians just because we speak that way in the house, just because we say in the house what every member in whose consituency there are farmers would say to them when he speaks publicly in his constituency.
The hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) said that with regard to some matters the minister said "yes" and his officials gave an answer directly opposite. I shall apply to these men, to Major General Pearkes, to Brigadier Mess and to all those ejusdem jarinae what the minister has just said with regard to imperialists and jingoes. "There are two classes in this country who make it difficult: first"-and this applies to Pearkes, Mess and the others-"those who are insistent on conscription whether we can get volunteers or not. Consciously or unconsciously, they discourage volunteer recruiting by constantly keeping up the agitation, criticizing and disparaging the efforts of those who are loyally giving their best efforts to persuade and urge young men of Canada to enlist." This applies to those men, and if Major General Pearkes deserves special consideration as a V.C., I suggest that he should exchange places with my friend Filip Konowal, V.C., and come down and clean the spittoons in the House of Commons and give the command in British Columbia to Filip Konowal, V.C. I think that would be the real thing. I have been fighting alone for Filip Konowal; I want recognition for him.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Shame.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Put Filip Konowal elsewhere. We are told sometimes that some officers are not bilingual when the men speak only one other language. That is not fair. An officer must understand the language of his mSn. There is no reason why a man should have an interpreter to speak to at least one of his officers. There is one thing that
The Budget-Mr. Pouliot

any hon. gentleman who has been in the army knows very well, namely, that as soon as a man gets into the army, whether he has volunteered or not, he thinks of home; he wants to go home on his first leave. He wants his leave. There have been times when leaves have been refused men because they did not volunteer.
I have here a few notes of what is being done in the line of persuasion to induce men to volunteer by making appeals to their reason. You will be surprised, sir. It is something shameful. In the first place they have one forty-eight hour leave in two months. Formerly I think they had one forty-eight hour and one thirty-six hour leave per month. In the second place sleeping-out passes of the N.R.M.A. men are cancelled. Third, perma-ment leave until midnight is cancelled, which means that the soldiers cannot go to the movies, theatre concerts, et cetera. They cannot go to those concerts outside the camp, since they have to leave the hall around nine-thirty. Fourth, names are called in the huts at ten o'clock to prevent N.R.M.A. men from going to free movies given at the camp four times weekly. If a soldier is five minutes late he goes to the clink. Volunteers are sent to the clink only if absent for more than twenty-one days or if drunk. But if a man is called a zombie or a dead-living man is five minutes late he is sent to the clink. Fifth, access to playgrounds is forbidden to them. They have no right to play tennis, baseball, or anything. Sixth, they are forbidden to go to the beer canteen even though they are thirsty. I find that awful. Seventh, they are put in separate huts. They eat in the same kitchens but at separate tables to humiliate them. They are exposed to jeers and sneers from those who have volunteered and who say that they are cowards, do not have the guts to volunteer. Eighth, they are forbidden to attend dances, games of bridge or any other social activity for the recreation of the soldier. Ninth, free time and leisure time for others and week-ends are employed in dirty work. Sundays-that July 2-N.R.M.A. men were working with pick and shovel part of the afternoon at Barriefield, eighty miles from Ottawa.
1 have a few notes here which were taken in 'May at the camp at Lauzon. The men had nothing to do. They were kept like prisoners in cells just because they did not volunteer, although the minister explained this afternoon that these men are doing excellent work, but they have no recreation. They are like friars who have made the three vows, and Have no distraction. It is not surprising that they dislike the army and that some of them are
[Mr. Pouliot.l
deserters. I understand it very well. Why are there facilities for entertaining all soldiers? It is precisely to make them just as happy as possible in the army. But all that is cancelled because these men do not sign for overseas. They act in conformity with the law which is in force at the present time, and they are punished for that; they are humiliated and we are still told that there is no conscription. There is conscription, of course; there is conscription by the back door, and it has been condemned by the Globe and Mail. They were perfectly right in condemning it. The trouble is that we are far away from realities. We must know what is meant by conscription. If we mean by conscription, and it is the spirit as well as the letter of the law, that a man or a woman should be at the place where he or she can serve best in the war effort nobody will object to that. But the trouble is that some people understand by conscription only the sending of men overseas, paying no attention to the usefulness of the farmers, the railwaymen or the men in the munitions factories and all the men who are essential to the war effort. That is the difficulty. When a member of parliament, or a journalist or anyone else says that it is wrong, that we cannot go very far with an unbalanced, one-sided war effort, that we need a balanced war effort, then immediately that person is told he is a bad Canadian and does not appreciate what Should be done during this war.
I am perhaps the one member who has said the most to try to. encourage the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) and to give him a superiority complex. I still maintain, sir, that the man who must carry the burden, of the man-power problem during the war is not the Minister of Defence (Mr. Ralston); it is the Minister of Labour. He should not have the position of a hyphen between the Department of National Defence and industry. He should be the judge, the man who will decide the usefulness of every man.
No complaint whatever should be favourably received unless it is proved to his satisfaction that the men asked for by the army are really needed. I cannot understand hon. gentlemen opposite, who always agree with any commitment that may be made with regard to the size of the army. They never blame the Minister of National Defence for the size of the Canadian army, which is larger than during the last war. It is out of proportion, because we are making more munitions than we did during the last war, and we are feeding more countries than we did then. Hon. gentlemen opposite do not take those facts into consideration; they are

The Budget-Mr. Knowles
ready to destroy this country probably just for an electoral argument. They should do better than that. They cannot go on in that way, putting politics into the question of man-power and all these other matters. It would be unbelievable. Then I should like to say that many soldiers are given punishment that is out of proportion to the offence, and when the sentence is served the men are found unfit, although they have been kept in the clink for a long time. Some men have been imprisoned for two years or more, during which time they, were no good to the army or to the country. When any complaints are made, the commanding officer is supreme.
In closing, sir, I should like to define my own Liberalism by quoting a telegram which I sent to the secretary of the Liberal youth convention at Winnipeg on May 29:
Admirable and fortunate youths who sincerely believe in the Liberal creed and who have not yet lost the gift of speech, I salute you from our national capital, where my parliamentary duties are preventing me from attending your convention.
Be sure that you will remain young so long as your heart remains young. Never forget that anyone is disqualified for public service the very day he becomes vain and selfish. Always forget yourself to think of and for your fellow countrymen.
We have every reason to be proud of the pioneers and builders of Liberalism who gladly suffered poverty and humiliation while fighting the family compact. They promoted democracy and established a responsible government. Make their doctrine your own.	.
You will gain prestige in keeping your personality true to itself. Do not let anyone extinguish in your heart the sacred flame of enthusiasm. Take your inspiration from the immortal speeches of the great Liberal leaders of the past and compare your notes with what is said to-day.
In these materialistic times when countless opportunists worship the golden calf, do not rely on hearsay for your appreciation of current events. Weigh what is said and what is done. Remember that freedom of speech is the very essence of Liberalism. Never be afraid to make your own judgment and to defend your own views until one proves to the satisfaction of your mind that you are not right.
Do not judge anyone by what he is, but by what he accomplishes. To quote the great Laurier, be adamant with the haughty, but do not fail to be kind, generous and helpful to the sick and the needy, in order that the Liberal party never ceases to be the people's party. Public respect will be your reward.
Liberalism shall never die. Liberalism shall never be a meaningless word. If it ever became a smoke-screen for lobbyists, profiteers and theatrical producers, would it not ,be an outrage to the glorious past of the Liberal party?
A large number of well gifted and promising young men are in the Canadian forces. Those who will survive this terrible war and yourselves will have the duty to join together in a
patriotic and common effort to establish "the new order" which everybody speaks of and which nobody knows.
The task of reshaping the destiny of out beloved country, Canada, is formidable. It is yours. Do not be downhearted. You may succeed and you will do so, but only if you are imbued with Christian charity and with a true Canadian spirit, and if you are guided by the sound principles of true. Liberalism.

speakeroldname: Mr. S. H. KNOWLES (Winnipeg North Centre):
speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to
return to the subject that is now before the house; I refer to the consideration of this year's budget, which was presented to parliament by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Iisley) on June 26. Like other hon. members who have spoken, there are certain points concerning which I should like to congratulate the minister. I agree with him in the basic considerations which he singled out as those that had to be faced in formulating this year's budget proposals. There were four, as indicated at page 4174 of Hansard: first, meeting the cash requirements; second, encouraging production; thiid, relieving cases of special hardship in the matter of income taxation; fourth, facing up to the need of a plan for the post-war period. I feel, too, that I want to congratulate the minister upon the clarity with which he states his position as far as the post-war period is concerned. I do not agree with the position he takes, but I could wish that other hon. members would follow his example and discuss objectively and straightforwardly the basic issues before us as we look into the post-war period, instead of indulging in diatiibes and criticisms of one kind or another against the principles of democratic control of industry and public ownership. Both in this debate and in the debate that took place a short time ago on the second reading of the Bank Act the minister made his position quite clear. He also made it clear that in his mind there is an issue as between private enterprise and the public ownership and control which this party proposes, and that this is the issue which will have to be settled in the immediate postwar period.
In a few minutes I shall come back to what the minister had to say along that line. Before doing so, I wish to say something about the financial proposals which the minister has presented on the basis of his first three considerations. First of all, I should like to speak about the suggestion that the compulsory savings portion of the personal income tax be discontinued. The minister pointed out in his speech that this action will mean a loss of revenue to the government in the amount of about $110,000,000 a year. In other words the minister has told the house and the
The Budget-Mr. Knowles

country that in the light of the protests which have been made and the grievances that need to be adjusted it is possible to make adjustments in the budget for this year to the tune of $110,000,000. Accordingly, when we in this corner of the house make certain suggestions we are not asking for money which is not there. We are merely proposing alternative ways of making adjustments with that 5110,000,000. Basically our contention is that if there is that amount of money with which adjustments can be made, the full benefit of it should go to those who need it most, namely to those in the lower income brackets. That is the reason why, even though we welcome in the name of the people who will get some relief this proposal of the minister, we have contended that alternative measures would have been better. We feel that the whole amount of that $110,000,000 should have been given by way of relief to those in the lower income brackets.
When different speakers supporting the amendment of the Progressive Conservative party, and hon. members from other parts of the house, have suggested that the income tax exemption level should be raised, the reply of the minister has been that if that were done it would result in huge savings of income tax for those in the higher brackets. This was said, too, by the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent). I would point out that when the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) spoke he said that if an adjustment such as we are proposing were to be made, there would have to be an adjustment of the rates in the higher brackets, so that what was feared would not happen. In other words, there is no real argument on the point; it is just a matter of arithmetic, or a matter of adjusting the rates. AVe contend that if there is this amount of money with which adjustments can be made, the full benefit of it should go to those in the lower income tax brackets.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Does that include the hon. member?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No; I refer to a lower bracket than the one in which we happen to come. Our problem is one of a special type, as the hon. minister knows.
As a matter of fact a small portion of that $110,000,000-perhaps seven, eight or ten millions-might have been used to give a further increase in old age pensions. I mention that as being in line with what I have already said, that if there is this amount of money with which to make adjustments, certainly no portion of that benefit should go to those in the upper brackets who do not need 
it, but who will get a measure of relief under the government's plan. The whole of it should go to those who need it.
There are a number of details I should like to call to the attention of the Minister of Finance or, in some cases, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Gibson). Their work, so far as income tax matters are concerned, is pretty much allied. I hold in my hand a copy of a notice sent to an income tax payer at a Toronto address. I need not give his name, but I have the actual document in my hand. It is dated June 6, 1944, and is identified as form T-218. This notice advised the taxpayer in question that his 1941 income tax had finally been assessed, and that it had been found that when he made out his income tax return for 1941 it was one cent short. So that, according to this statement, he now owes for 1941 the amount of one cent. But the form goes on to show that, in addition to the one cent, he _ owes interest. I hope members of the banking and commerce committee are not listening to this, because it may put ideas in their heads. It states that he owes interest on one cent amounting to $3.33, or a total debt of $3.34.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Incidentally, this taxpayer tells me that he was puzzled as to how he should make out his return in 1942, for the year 1941. He went to the office of the income tax people in Toronto, and had them help him1 make it out. The one cent mistake was their mistake, in the first place.

The Budget-Mr. Knowles
There is another matter I would call to the attention of these two ministers. This arose out of an unfortunate experience which was drawn to my attention a few months ago. A taxpayer in Winnipeg received notice that he stil'l owed S10 on his taxes for 1942. He was satisfied that he had paid the tax in full, and had his receipts. When he took the receipts to the Winnipeg office he was confronted with the blunt statement that his receipt in one instance did not conform to the records in the office, and he was told that he must have tampered with that receipt. The man was so incensed that he came to see me immediately, and I in turn took up the matter with the income tax authorities in Ottawa. May I say at this point that the income tax authorities here took care of the matter to my entire satisfaction and to the satisfaction of the taxpayer. In due course he was given a definite apology for some of the things that had been said to him.
But the point I call to the attention of the department is that that mistake could not have happened if a very simple change were made in the form of the receipt that is issued. What I say holds true to-day with respect to the receipts for such income tax payments as some of us are still making. The receipts have room only for the insertion of the amount in figures. There is no room for inserting the amount in words, by way of confirmation. If that very simple change were made, a change which it seems to me ought to be made in connection with income tax receipts, incidents such as the one I have described could not occur.
Another matter to which I would refer has already been mentioned in the debate by at least two hon. members. I refer to the request of parents of student nurses for income tax exemption on their account. This matter has been drawn to the attention of the authorities on a number of occasions. During the earlier part of the year I was in correspondence with both the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Revenue. In fact, in the house on May 19, during the discussion of another matter which had some bearing on the point, I asked1 the Minister of National Revenue whether something was being done, and his reply as it appears at page 3087 of Hansard for May 19, was:
The matter has been brought to the attention of the Minister of Finance and I know he is giving it consideration at the present time.
Well, that was not a commitment on the part of the Minister of Finance, but I must say that after that statement I was disappointed when this grievance was not taken care of under the third of the minister's basic considerations.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: A different minister said it, though.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
But the matter had been referred to the Minster of Finance. As a matter of fact I had correspondence from him in which he made a similar statement.
Another point under the third consideration outlined by the minister has to do with sleeping-car conductors and sleeping-car porters. As hon. members may know-for most of us have a good deal of contact with these gentlemen, as we travel around the country- they are treated differently, in one income tax matter, from railway engineers, firemen, brake-men and train conductors. These latter men to whom I have referred are allowed certain exemptions for their expenses while away from home. That allowance is denied to sleeping-car conductors and sleeping-car porters. I shall not take the time to give the technical basis for the discrimination, but it seems to me that something should be done to bring the situation into line as between these two groups. Here again I was in correspondnece with the two ministers to whom I have referred, and on May 30 the Minister of Finance wrote me in reply to one of my letters about a case of this ldnd and said:
I shall be glad to see that your representations are given careful consideration in the prebudgetary discussions which are now taking place.
Yours very truly,
J. L. Ilsley.
That was not a commitment, but the very fact that the matter was to be given consideration made me feel that there was some hope. Again I was. disappointed that the minister did not include a correction of that grievance when the budget was brought down.
Still another situation to which I should like to refer is the discrimination as between various pension plans when it comes to exemption from total income in the filing of income tax returns. This has been brought to my attention in particular by employees of the two railways, the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National. There are some plans the payments into which are exempted from total income before income tax is paid, while there are other pension plans where that allowance is not granted. I appreciate the minister's statement on this whole matter and I have given it close study. I notice it is his intention to set up a commission to study this subject, but in the meantime these employees feel that there is a marked discrimination
46S0
The Budget-Mr. Knowles

against them which I feel the minister might have taken care of this year. My time will not permit me to argue the case in detail, but I hope that even yet the minister will reconsider a number of matters like this, before the budget resolutions are finally passed.
There is still another grievance under clause 3 of the minister's basic considerations. On several occasions I have raised in the house the matter of income tax deductions from the men who went to lviska. After some considerable time the Minister of National Revenue made an announcement in which he concurred with my request. That announcement was most welcome, but there was such a long delay in making it that these men had already had taken away from them taxes which should not have been deducted. In the meantime some of these men have gone overseas, and deductions which were made in January, February and March of this year and which should not have been made; and which the government is now admitting will go back to them, are still being withheld. It looks to these men, if they live, as though they will not get these rebates until some time in 1946. I have taken this matter up several times with the department, but I urge that this matter could be expedited to an extent of which there has not yet been sufficient evidence.
I should like to turn for a moment to some of the comments I was making earlier when I congratulated the minister upon his clarity in stating his position so far as the post-war period was concerned. He has made it clear in this and other debates that he feels that the basis upon which to found post-war Canada is that of a return to the power and authority of private enterprise, private industry and private business. As a matter of fact, business itself is complaining that it is not getting everything it wants out of this budget, but at least the green light is there, the hint, the indication that if business will stick with the Liberal party it will get the full consideration it wants when the post-war period comes. The minister is unlike many other hon. members in that he faces up to the issue that has to be settled as between the return to the power and authority of private enterprise and the forward march to democratic public control of the economic life of the country in the interests of the people of Canada.

When the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Matthews) rose to speak this afternoon I thought he might deal with the matter about which he questioned the Minister of National Defence a week or two ago; I refer to the destruction in Brandon of material formerly used by the army at the A-4 centre which was closed there a short while ago. The hon. member a couple of weeks ago asked a question on the orders of the day about this. I have received considerable correspondence concerning it. In view of the fact that the hon. member for Brandon had asked the question I have refrained from raising the matter, thinking he would pursue it, and I thought he would certainly do so to-day. Apparently he has accepted the minister's answer, which he made, I believe, on Friday, to the effect that these things-enamel ware, porcelain ware and so on-w'ere destroyed for medical reasons. One of the correspondents I have had in connection with this matter from the city of Brandon is a medical doctor. He of course, as might be expected, ridicules the idea that these things could not have been sterilized, and I may say that the people of Brandon, according to the information I have, and the people of Winnipeg, 130 miles away, are quite indignant over this destruction of goods which could have been used-kinds of goods which are not available for civilian purchase in Manitoba at the present time. I have in my hand a copy of the Winnipeg Tribune of July 7 which contains photographs of some of these go^ds, showing that the axe

The Budget-Mr. Cruickshank
has been put right through them to destroy them and make sure that they could not be used.
I have not the time to go into this matter in greater detail, but the answer given by the Minister of National Defence does not satisfy the local people in Brandon or the people of Manitoba generally, and I think the whole question of the disposal of army and canteen goods calls for further investigation at this stage, so that if there has been anything amiss in this incident the situation will not be repeated. I am perplexed to understand it in the light of the action which this parliament took in setting up the War Assets Corporation. I wonder why it is that these goods were not declared surplus and turned over to that corporation for sale or disposal in some orderly way. It has been called to my attention that some of these articles such as coal scuttles, garbage cans, et cetera, which missed the axe when they were thrown on the dump in Brandon, have been retrieved by Brandon citizens and are now being used. The people are glad to get them and sterilize them and make use of them, because such articles are not available on the market there at the present time. I hope the Minister of National Defence or the Minister of Munitions and Supply will look into this matter further, so that if there has been anything amiss it can be corrected before there is a recurrence of it.

May I say to the house, through you, Mr. Speaker, that this is not going to be a speech like most of those that have been made in this budget debate, a speech which someone reads that has been written by someone else. I have no notes; I have nothing written, and any time I have to have my speech written by somebody else it will not be made in this house. I am sorry to say that does not go for at least eighty-five per cent of the members, and I do not need to look very far afield when I say that, or in any particular corner of the house. I cannot understand how any member of this house, being a returned soldier, can refrain from taking part in this debate. I am sorry that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) is not in the house, because what I have to say is concerned primarily with his department. Possibly there might be an election, and after hearing all the delightful figures from Winnipeg I wish to put myself on record now before that election.
Mr. Speaker, in the few years that I have been in Ottawa I have been treated with great courtesy by yourself, by the Clerk, and by every official of the House of Commons and every senior official of the civil service with whom I have come in contact, and on this occasion I wish to express my appreciation of all these courtesies that have been shown me. And let me say that I have no hope of getting a judgeship.
The reason why I am speaking now is that, as I understand, it is desired to have the vote taken to-night. I certainly would not have spoken to-night if I had thought that the vote would be taken to-morrow; I would have preferred to wait until then. However, let me say that I have listened throughout this debate in connection with the budget to everything except the budget. Everything but the budget has been discussed, and I have heard now something that I had not expected to hear discussed even by my hon. friends
The Budget-Mr. Cruickshank

from Winnipeg-the groom of the bedchamber. The reason why I am not going to vote against the government on this occasion is this. Frankly, I had expected that I would vote against the government on the budget because I did not see how I could do otherwise as a returned soldier. The Progressive Conservatives would have received my support if their amendment had been framed in different language. I would have been voting with them, but I cannot vote with them as the amendment stands. I entirely disagree with the government on their man-power policy and am not afraid to say so, but I must say at the same time that every party in this house made the same mistake in 1940. The Cooperative Commonwealth Federation did not want to take any part in the war at all.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The Liberal party, however, made a mistake-and I am a supporter of the Liberal party. The National Conservative party of that day, whose name has been changed about eleven times since then, would also not take any action. The fact of the matter is that none of us was prepared to face the public and say that we would put conscription into force from the drop of the hat, although we represented the people of Canada.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You might admit it.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have listened to you people making your speeches about $25 a month several times and I want you to listen to my speech about S25 an hour. None of the parties had courage to face the public and say that it would put conscription into force at the very outset, as the United States and Great Britain did. We all made a mistake, and I include myself. But surely we should have the courage now to admit our mistake. There is one thing I cannot understand in public life and it is this. Wre speak of His Majesty's Loyal Opposition, but what do they do? If the government adopts any of their better ideas they immediately begin to cry because those ideas have been adopted, but that is what the opposition is for. The greatest mistake that any man in public life can make is, in my opinion, not to.be willing to admit that he has been in error. We who are in public life in Canada, I repeat, all made a mistake in 1940 when we failed to adopt the right attitude in this matter. But to-day it is a different story. I said in 1940, speaking as an old soldier, that in my opinion one volunteer was worth any ten conscripts. I attempt to keep up to date even with my hon. friend and his programme. I keep up to date. I can change my opinion in that regard. I say now that any one man of the 29th battalion is worth forty conscripts. I am now going four times better than before. We have this army here. A short time ago I was not prepared to adopt the attitude that I am adopting here. I really believe that at least the three ministers of national defence of the government think exactly the same as I do, but they are not ,in a position to speak out as freely. I believe that we should immediately put into effect the order in council, except for one reason. I believe it would cause more disunity in Canada than the forty thousand men are worth.
I am very much riled when I read in the newspapers and when I get first-hand information, that has not yet been contradicted by any member of the government, that soldiers of the Canadian army have been insulted in Valleyfield and in other parts of the province of Quebec and that the civilian authorities take no steps to stop these insults. I was told the other day by a woman serving in the armed forces from one province that when they are granted their furloughs they will not go home because they fear and hesitate to go to their own, districts, knowing that insults will be thrown at them for wearing the uniform. There is no use in trying to deny these facts. They are here and cannot be denied. When I say that, I know what I am talking about. Farmers' sons in British Columbia do not get the consideration that is given to farmers' sons in Quebec. I do not ask for that consideration for the farmers' sons in my riding, and I come from a farm riding. I am very proud of the fact that I come from a farm riding. We are proud of the fact that our sons are over there fighting to defend not Canada but the whole free world. We ask for no special consideration.
I do not like to say anything about the good province that I have defended every time
fMr. Cruickshank.!

The Budget-Mr. Cruickshank
I have gone home, but I for one am tired of hearing this talk about unity, if unity is to be only one-sided. There are nine provinces in Canada. If we are to have unity we must have unity of the whole nine provinces, not one province against the eight. We cannot afford under any consideration to do anything that would bring on disunity now; but I want that one province to remember this, a day of reckoning will come unless a different attitude is adopted in their responsibility as a part of Canada, and they will regret it far more than the rest of Canada.
There is one thing that I heartily disagree with the Department of National Defence on, and again I am sorry the minister is not at the moment in his place but he knows my stand on it. To-day the minister told us the one great thing that we want to keep in the wonderful army is unity and esprit de corps, exactly as we had in the last war. He told us that he wanted to keep the army up to strength. I agree with him 100 per cent. He told us that in his opinion, from a voluntary point of view-and he is not only speaking as Minister of National Defence but as a soldier with a distinguished record in the last war-a volunteer far outshone any conscript. That can be checked in Hansard to-morrow. I agree with him 100 per cent. Where I do disagree with him and his department most emphatically is that in Petawawa to-day volunteers have to take orders from conscript non-commissioned officers. Mr. Speaker, that is not good enough in this day and age, That will not go down before the boys. Figures were quoted to-day by the minister, but I happen to know that volunteers in Petawawa and other camps have to take orders from a draftee who will not or cannot see his way clear to do his duty for his country. That is one point that rankles most with me, and I think this government would be well advised, if they wish to have any standing whatsoever with the men who are serving overseas, to rectify this at once, and to see to it that no volunteers are asked to take orders from a draftee who will not volunteer to serve his country wherever his services are needed.
Mr. Speaker, it is usually customary to praise the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsey) on his budget speech, but as far as I can see, everything but the budget has been discussed today; therefore, I prefer to praise the two ministers that I think should be given most credit in connection with the budget. I have disagreed with the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) on many occasions and perhaps will do so on many more; but I wish to tell him that in my opinion, as a representative of a rural riding-and I would say this in my riding before Liberal, Conservative or C.C.F.
members-no other man in this House of Commons has the knowledge of agriculture that he has. I shall not always agree with him, but I wish to praise him for his part in this budget. I shall not tell the house how long I have been connected with politics, because I might be giving away my age, but ever since I have been connected with it, or ever since I remember my father speaking of it, what we were fighting for was the removal of the duty from farm implements. What happened in this budget? The present Minister of Agriculture by his steadfast fighting secured this action on our behalf.
There is another minister to whom I wish to give a word of praise, and possibly I am sticking my neck out in a political sense in British Columbia by saying this, but I do not care. I am a charter member of the Canadian Legion, and I wish to tell hon. members here that any member of the Canadian Legion is allowed to speak for the soldiers not only of the last war, but of this war. I happen to belong to a few organizations. A person can belong to an organization by right of might or by right of wealth or by some other right, but there is only one organization in Canada to which one can belong by only one right, his right of service for his king and country, namely, the Canadian Legion. Make no mistake about that. I may be criticized by some of the branches in my province in what I am about to say of the minister to whom I shall refer in a moment. He has taken a lot of criticism. He has even taken some from the city of Toronto about a hospital, but I am very proud of the fact that each and every party in this house have given nothing but praise to the present Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) for his efforts on behalf of the soldiers. I do not always agree with the legislation he has brought down, neither do the legion. But I wish to assure the legion, through you, Mr. Speaker, that if they knew the Minister of Pensions and National Health as I know him they would know that, while we have not got all that we endeavoured to get, we would not have got half of what we have secured had it not been for the sympathetic efforts of the minister.
I wish to make a suggestion to the government. I hope there is to be a vote, although it has been intimated to me since I began to speak that there will not be one to-night. That being so, I may take my forty minutes. I should like to say a little about some of the problems of agriculture. I wish the Minister of Finance were in his place at present, because I could give him some advice
The Budget-Mr. Cruickshank

that I trust he will take. If he took it he would have a far more successful operating board in one of those temporary buildings- thank goodness they call them "temporary". Let us hope they will be temporary. In saying that I do not wish to be critical of the board. They have done wonderful work. The only suggestion I wish to make to the Minister of Finance with respect to his part in the budget is that he adopt the principle they have adopted in the United States with respect to their board corresponding 'to our wartime prices and trade board. In the United States their board meets with all the farm organizations and the cooperatives, not after they fix the price of strawberries-and while the Minister of Finance is not listening, I think the Minister of Agriculture is-but before they fix the price of strawberries and vegetables. The board meets with the farmers and others and gets their ideas on what they should be paid, what they think the farmers can produce for. What does our board do? They do not even meet when they fix the prices. They do not meet at all, and when they send their officials out to Brtiish Columbia they ignore them afterwards. The sad part so far as the berry growers in British Columbia are concerned is unfortunately the Minister of Agriculture was out in Saskatchewan on a forlorn mission at the time the berries were picked. I am sorry that because of the freight rates problem, or because of the heat it is not possible to send British Columbia berries here. It would be a revelation to hon. members if I could give them a real meal of British Columbia strawberries; they would remember it for a long time. I want, however, to pay tribute to one hon. member. The other day I happened to be up in the "bucket of blood", where I remarked that I had not eaten a good piece of meat since coming back to eastern Canada. One of my good C.C.F. friends, who was going back to his farm a day or two later, brought me a really good roast of beef, and I want to say that you could not get finer beef anywhere in Canada, with the exception of the province of British Columbia.
I see the Minister of National Defence is back in the house, and I want to offer a criticism. In doing so I am speaking most emphatically for the old soldiers I- know. I know I am speaking for many soldiers serving overseas at the present time. I think I am speaking for the Canadian Legion. I know definitely I am speaking for the battalion of which I am very proud, the 29th, which was mentioned by the minister to-day when speaking of esprit de corps. In no less than three letters received to-day from over-
seas and letters from twio army camps in Canada I am told that I speak for soldiers on active service both here and abroad when I say both the old soldiers and the soldiers engaged in the present war strongly resent what neither the Minister of National Defence nor any other minister can defend; that is, the fact that a non-commissioned officer of the draftee army, who does not wear the G.S., can give orders to a private who does wear it. No govemrhent, no party and no individual can defend that as far as I am concerned.
I have another suggestion to offer the minister. According to this week's issue of Time the government of the United States is giving its soldiers another raise in pay. Speaking from memory I believe it is to be $10 a month for the highest grades in the infantry, and it is estimated that seventy-five per cent of the infantry will come within that category. I want to recommend to the minister that he immediately increase the pay of members of. the active army serving in theatres of war by fifty cents a day, to be given either as a deferred payment in the form of war savings certificates or in the form of a life insurance policy. Do not let the sound money men talk you out of it; pay no attention to the Bank of Canada. I am sure the people of Canada will 'be behind you. You cannot buy patriotism, but yiou can reward gallant service. You will have the support of all the people, no matter what their political party. The people of Canada will never begrudge an extra fifty cents a day to our fighting men. You cannot pay for the sacrifice a man makes when he loses his life, but you can give him some reward in this way. I want to urge this upon the minister for his consideration, and I do not believe it could be classed as a bribe to anyone. It is our duty to differentiate in some way between those who are offering their lives and those who are staying at home.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, speaking in the house last session on the subject of man-power I said that I agreed with those who had declared that in a free society the obligations and privileges of military training should be shared generally under a fair and just system of selective compulsory service without geographical restriction. I am convinced now, as I was then, that this is the correct policy. I read afterwards that I was as a voice calling in the wilderness, and perhaps it might have seemed that way because, if I remember aright, I received very little support from hon. members sitting in this house in opposition to the government. The exception, as was mentioned a few moments

The Budget

Mr. Gray
ago, was the New Democracy party which, ever since the outbreak of war, has urged that there should be compulsory selective service without geographical restriction. As for the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, the only group in this house which opposed as a group the passing of what was then known as bill No. 80, the National Resources Mobilization Act, introduced by the government to remove the restrictions with respect to service overseas, and which party, as my hon. friend has just said, was opposed to the sending of any expeditionary force to the aid of the motherland after the outbreak of war in 1939, that party stands indicted to-day by its failure to meet the challenge and perform its duty when called upon at that time. I propose to place on record the words of the leader of the C.C.F. party speaking in this house at the war session of 1939, as they are found at page 55 of Hansard of that year:
In view of these considerations, the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation believes that Canada's policy should be based first on the fundamental national interests of the Canadian people, as well as on their interest in the outcome of war. Canada should be prepared to defend her own shores, but her assistance overseas should be limited to economic aid and must not include conscription of man-power or the sending of any expeditionary force.
I repeat, "or the sending of any expeditionary force." What hope have we, therefore, from a party which in time of peril would interpret Canada's interests in the most narrow and restricted sense; a party which, at the very moment British, Canadian and United States troops were struggling to maintain a foothold on the Normandy beaches, in conference assembled, presided over by a leader of the party and having as its guest the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), would pass the following resolution:
Whereas the C.C.F. is a socialist party, and whereas the official policy of the British labour party of coalition with the Conservative party compromised the working class struggle against capitalism in Great Britain, therefore be it resolved that the Quebec C.C.F. declares strong disapproval of the continuation of its policy of collaboration with the capitalistic government of Great Britain.
Instead of condemning, let us give credit to the labour party in Great Britain which, in the empire's darkest hour, was willing to postpone for the time being its hopes for the future in order to retain the objectives already won. To-day I find some support from the official opposition, but it is a timid support tucked in at the very end of a long resolution moved in amendment to the budget, and only conceived after forty-seven days of almost continuous debate on the war appropriation measure. Surely some time during the weeks that debate
lasted the official opposition could have made a motion in plain, clear, unequivocal terms instead of leaving it to the budget debate and the financial critic who, after spending ninety-five per cent of his time in discussing fiscal matters, dealt with the man-power question only incidentally. I submit, further, that the amendment is not a definite resolution that the government enforce the powers contained in chapter 13 of the 1940 statutes, being the general mobilization resources act, as amended by chapter 29 of the 1942 statutes, commonly known as bill No. 80. Let me read the amendment moved by the official opposition:
That the government has failed to make effective the full mobilization of our financial, industrial and material resources, as well as our man-power, but is maintaining a so-called home-defence army, at a cost to the taxpayer in excess of $150 million per annum, at a time when the need for army reinforcements, for farming and for industry is so urgent.
What that means perhaps the mover alone could tell. But if one reads the clause and couples with it the statement made by the hon. member, wherein he urges that we turn these men back to farms, factories and forests until needed, it must mean the disbandment of these highly-trained men. With this sentiment I disagree, with all the force at my command; and I am in full accord with the remarks of the Minister of National Defence this afternoon and those of the hon. member for Brantford City (Mr. Macdonald) who, speaking in this house last week in the debate, said that he would oppose with all his strength the demobilization of these fully-trained forces.
I noticed in Hansard that when the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. May-bank) was speaking the other evening, the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) interrupted him, and said that he was being misinterpreted. The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre was interpreting the remark in a manner similar to what I have done, saying that the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe had said that the men should be sent back to the farms, the factories and the forests. That hon. member said he was being misinterpreted. Therefore, in order that there may be no mistake, and to keep the record clear, let me quote exactly what was said by the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe, and let the house be the judge. His remarks are found at page 4341 of Hansard for June 29, as follows:
For the honour of Canada I urge upon the government that they now remove the political halo that surrounds this most ridiculous camouflage and to turn these able-bodied men back to the farms, the factories and the forest where they can produce for victory until they are marshalled for the more vital service for which they were conscripted.
The Budget-Mr. Gray

The minister, speaking today, was too kind when he said that they were to be sent back to the farms, the forests, the factories or for service overseas. No; according to the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe, they are to be sent back to the farms, the forests and the factories.
And for how long?-"Until they are marshalled for the more vital service." Can anyone imagine anything more fantastic than to demobilize these men, to use the words of the hon. member, "until they are marshalled for the more vital service?" It is true that we have heard from the hustings from a reported leader of the party that the Progressive Conservatives were going to lay down the gauntlet and call for an immediate order in council. This, however, came from the outside, from a gentleman who has no responsibility to parliament, and not from the elected leader in this house. I ask this chamber: Is it significant that we have had no direct endorsement of the statements made by Mr. McTague and Mr. Bracken? Is it significant that the elected leader in this chamber has remained silent in the matter, up to this time?
I submit that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) is right when he states that such statements of policy should be made by the leader in this house, where the statements may be analysed, and not made from positions of ambush. I am not prepared to say, as did Mr. McTague, that the province of Quebec would vote otherwise than it did if now given an opportunity. At the same time 1 have faith enough in the loyalty of French Canada, when the need is properly shown and when it realizes that all the seventy-odd thousands of men now mobilized and fully trained are being treated in the same manner. Then, with few exceptions, the whole subject will be looked upon in its proper light, and these men will go out and do battle with their fellow men, and come back proud that the step was taken and that they were privileged to form a part of the Canadian Army in the restoration and liberation of a free France, and the conquest of a German tyrant.
I listened carefully to the speech of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) this afternoon. I know how proud he is, as are we all, of the volunteer forces; we know the sincerity of purpose of the minister. Those of us who have had the privilege of volunteering for service to our country, wherever called, remember the thrill of pride when first we donned the uniform. At the same time, as I have said in this house before: Is it a fair system? Is it a just fMr. Grav.]
system? Is it fair that one family should offer its all, and another family not give anything?
Nor do I think-and I say this in all kindness-it is fair for the minister to use as an illustration in support of the citizen committees for recruiting, the use of these same bodies by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) in connection with his victory loan. To me there is a vast difference between urging my neighbour or friend to invest his money in a gilt-edged victory bond, and in urging him to have his son enlist for active service. I still urge the government to enforce the statute by order in council, especially having in mind that the reserve forces are now well-trained and capable of being utilized, if necessary, as an active home defence force. At the same time, I do not propose to allow an amendment such as that moved by the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe to becloud the real issue in the debate, namely the support or otherwise of the fiscal policy of the government, as enunciated by the Minister of Finance. Therefore I shall vote against the amendment as framed by the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe, and I shall support the Minister of Finance in his motion to go into committee of ways and means.

Finance must be- secondary to other considerations in the winning of the war. I wish I could say the same of the government's settled policy in regard to the after-war years, and that whatever should prove to be physically possible and desirable should be made financially possible.
That is exactly what the government are doing now. The hon. member went on as though he expected the government to have appropriated $5,000 million this session, while the war is still going on, in order to prepare for the post-war period. I think the government are doing a wonderful job, and I am not flattering them when I say that. When I read the soldiers' rehabilitation bill as brought down by the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) I felt that he had done a marvellous job in benefiting by the experience of all the mistakes in the scheme which was enacted after the last war.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar went on, after talking about the application of a socialist policy:
_ I fear, however, and the present budget increases my fears, that the government is anxious to hurry back to the restrictive practices of orthodox finance and orthodox industry.
May I pause here to say that the socialism advocated by his party is the oldest kind of orthodoxy, the oldest system in the world, and that anybody who has taken time to read history knows that in every place and at every time it has been tried it has ended in disaster, bloodshed and ruin for the working people, and could have no other effect.
Some of us have at times entered the realm of prophecy. I recall that in the early part of the 1930 campaign Mr. Bennett-for whom I have great respect as a man of honesty and integrity-told the people of Canada that we were- importing too much. In the midst of the campaign he made the specific statement that we were over-importing by at least half a billion dollars. From that day on during my campaign I made the prediction, "If Mr. Bennett is returned to power, and does what he says he is going to do, before his term of office is up you will see in Canada at least one million unemployed; your wheat which was then selling for one dollar, will sell for twenty-five cents a bushel; your steers, now selling at $60, will sell for S10; your bacon hogs will sell for $2.50 a hundred." I made that prediction in July, 1930. Of course it did not impress very many people. A man came to me after a meeting and said, "Do you expect us to be impressed by that prediction?" I said, "No. I don't, but when it comes true will you come and see me?" Just t\yo years and five months later that man came to my office and with a tremor in his voice said, "My God, it has all come true."

The member for Rosetown-
Biggar said:
Before I make any proposal I wish to take exception to the reference made by the minister to taxation in other countries. Even supposing his comparisons happen to be fair, would the fact that another country overtaxes its poor justify Canada in following a similar course?
The minister was speaking of New Zealand in this case.
The minister stated that the New Zealand rates bear more heavily on low income brackets

The Budget-Mr. Ward
than do the rates in force in Canada, but what he did not say is that the New Zealand rates included the five per cent social security levy.
The Minister of Finance then said:
I did say that. ... I said that it included national security and social security taxes.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar then said:
I read the speech very carefully, and it must have escaped me.
There are many things that escape the hon. member. He goes on:
I say that the criticism that is often made of other countries does not take everything into account.
I would say, however, that if ever there was a case of the pot calling the stove black it was this case, because the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar is a past master at misrepresentation, at half-truths, at twisting and turning things to suit his own purpose. Then he cuts loose:
So I say that when we come to appraise what is happening in another country, let us be fair about it, and say what the people of that country are getting for the taxes they pay.
I would say to my hon. friends who smile about it that they have one stock-in-trade, and that is to engender fear in the minds of the people, to blacken their country, to blacken their own people, to blacken our Canadian institutions and public men. That is their chief stock-in-trade. I warn them that if they are ever charged with responsibility, the grave responsibility that falls upon a government called upon to administer this very difficult country of ours, spread four thousand miles east and west and only two or three hundred miles wide, with five or six different principalities, all with separate and different economics and climatic conditions- if they ever come to govern this country they will be sorry that they were not more responsible in the things they said in the days of opposition. I warn them of that.

I come now to the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright), and I pick him out for the reason that he pretends to speak at least for agriculture in his group. I will not take up the time of the house in reading much from his speech, but with reference to free agricultural implements, and again trying to belittle what has been accomplished, he says:
The freer exchange and export of goods has its place but, as I listen to the government members and read certain papers in this country, it seems to me that in placing responsibility for a prosperous Canada on export trade alone they are on very narrow ground indeed.
In reply I will call to witness some excellent organizations. First I will call as a witness the Canadian Legion in their admirable pamphlet on the question of rehabilitation of Canada's fighting men. This is what they say of trade:
This war has demonstrated that we have been able to keep our people employed and, within the limit of the basic supplies available, fed and clothed during a period of stress. We have, moreover, supplied our allies with the products of our own soil and resources. This provision, both for ourselves and others must, in view of the destruction and conditions throughout the rest of the world, continue for some considerable time.
They are willing to help our allies less fortunate than ourselves.
It may be that . . . through the brain and brawn of our workers, we have been able to do all this and yet maintain adequate living conditions in this country. Provided jobs are furnished the same condition can hold good in the post-war period while world trade is in process of rebuilding.
Note that, world trade.
Markets for all our products. Measures must be taken to explore and cultivate both domestic and foreign markets for our products. In foreign trade our aim should be to deal with countries that can supply things we require in our economy to satisfy our basic needs, and which we cannot or do not produce ourselves, or which we cannot or do not produce economically.
There is a good deal of excellent material in this book and they are solidly behind international trade.
Let me call yet another witness, an equally important body, the Canadian federation of agriculture. My hon. friend pretends to be speaking for agriculture. This is what they say in a pamphlet entitled "Principles of Post-War Reconstruction for Agriculture," published recently:
Though the farm problem is a domestic one in many respects, it is profoundly affected by, and to some extent dependent upon, international policies and action. More than ever before the effective solution of the problems of Canadian agriculture will hinge upon the planning of relations and upon the measure of agreement and cooperation which can be worked out between food exporting and food importing countries. Moreover, not merely policies having to do with food and agriculture enter into this but as well international policies governing trade generally, the payment of debts, the control and stabilization of currencies, and maintenance of peace.
Then they go on to say:
If we imagine we can return to the economic anarchy of the old days-
That is exactly what will happen. Anarchy is the right word if we ever attempt to socialize the industries of this young and growing country.
-then certainly we shall bring not only discredit but disaster upon ourselves and it will
The Budget-Mr. Ward

be well merited. None of us can now escape from revolutionary changes even if we would.
Then farther down they say:
In our opinion it is of little use to talk of reconstruction and rehabilitation plans for agriculture unless we assume the establishment of a fiscal policy and an international trade policy which will work in terms of the world of to-morrow.
They conclude by saying:
The united nations conference on food and agriculture^ held at Hot Springs, Virginia, in May of this year declared its belief: "that the goal of freedom from want of food suitable and adequate for the health and strength of all people can be achieved;" that the almost unlimited possibilities of an expanding world economy-
That does not sound like our C.C.F. friends talking about controlling economy1-
You would not understand our policies.

Living within ourselves. Get the hon. member for York South a funnel to talk through.
-should be organized and coordinated on a world scale; and that all nations, individually and collectively, should set about to achieve this broad objective.
That is, international trade.
Further, it recommended the establishment of a permanent international organization to promote and facilitate international cooperation dealing with problems of food and agriculture.
I do not need- to call in any more witness in that regard with the exception of one of the greatest statesmen on the north American continent, a member of the United States government who used these words within the last month. You will pardon me, Mr. Speaker, for referring to this since it is part of a broadcast I made a few weeks ago. Part of the material which I am about to quote is contained in the remarks of Mr. Sumner Welles, a great United States statesman and economist. This is what he said:
After the last war our high tariff policy-reached out to virtually every corner of the earth and brought poverty and despair to innumerable communities. But the effects on American importers, and on American industries dependent upon imports, were likewise immediate. Many foreign countries, which had not recovered from the shock of our tariff increases in 1921 and 1922 and were tottering on the *brink of economic and financial collapse were literally pushed into the abyss by our tariff action of 1930. Throughout the world this withering blast of _ trade destruction brought disaster and despair to countless millions of people.
That comes from a man who has been a member of the United States government for a long time. I shall continue with the quota-

tion of a page or two, Mr. Speaker, of my broadcast, because it is one on which I spent a lot of time and gathered a lot of figures:
The question is frequently asked, if we can do it in war time why cannot we do. it in peace time, meaning of course the employment of all our people. We can if the world will continue on a free trade basis as it is to-day. Of the almost five billion of international trade we did in 1943, a large percentage of it was on a free trade basis. The United States last year purchased from us 263 million bushels of grain, 244 millions of which entered their country with the same freedom as though there had been no international boundary.
There was no tariff on the 244 millions of bushels of grain.
This is true also of the vast supply of raw materials and munitions of war that flow to and from Canada to, not only the United States but to all the other nations with whom and for whom we are fighting.
The United States has to date this year purchased from us over 200 million bushels of Canadian grain, all of which will flow freely to their country without tariff or any other trade restrictions. Compare this condition with those of the early thirties when in many countries of Europe, especially those now under totalitarian governments tariffs ranged from one to two hundred per cent.
In pre-Hitler days prior to 1930 Germany's annual imports of grain-
And I verified those figures recently.

was rarely less than 100 million bushels. It consisted principally of barley, rye and oats. A very large part of which was purchased from Canada.
Italy's annual purchases of Canadian wheat in pre-Mussolini days averaged about 60,000.000 bushels. Spain too, before the revolution purchased annually about 35,000.000 bushels of wheat, most of it coming from Canada. France, also, was a fairly heavy buyer of Canadian hard spring wheat until in 1929 she placed a tariff of $1.19 per bushel against imports of foreign wheat. In all, this vast trade of over 200,000,000 bushels plus millions in other forms of trade vanished as mist before the morning sun, under the impact of high tariffs. Yes, even Canada and the United States in 1930 were caught in the psychological meshes of a world gone mad on the theory of high tariffs and self-sufficiency 

we too, followed suit with tariffs ranging from forty per cent to eighty per cent.
We all remember that.
By the early thirties the world had reached the logical conclusion to their insane policies of trade exclusion, a condition where every country in the world was trying to sell its goods but no country was buying. Can you visualize the loss to our trade and economy of over 200,000,000 bushels of grain sales annually-
Plus hundreds of millions of other trade.
In order that we may get an absolutely clear perspective of just what did happen during these awful early nineteen thirty years-world trade declined between 1928 and 19S-. from $9,640,000,000 to $2,234,000,000 or twenty-six per cent only of what it was five years previously when the world was on a more sane, more reasonable trading basis.

The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie (Lamb ton)
As an example of the effect on our Canadian trade of extremely high import duties not only in Europe but on this continent as well, in 1928 our external trade amounted to $2,586,106,275; by 1933 just five years later our total external trade had shrunk to $936,698,100 or thirty-two per cent only of what it was five years previously. ... To those who may still doubt the direct and inevitable relationship of high tariffs and unemployment

I recommend this to my hon. friends of the C.C.F. party.
-may X remind you that at no time in the world's history were tariffs anywhere nearly so high or did so many other obstructions exist in -trade as between 1929 -and the outbreak of war. Nor were there ever before in the world's history nearly so many unemployed.
Compare those days -and conditions with the freer trade policies w7e are enjoying to-day with the resultant comfort, satisfaction and pleasure of our people, -a market for everything we can produce, a job at good wages for every one who wants to work-our farmers selling their products at satisfactory prices with everybody living in a moderate state of luxury.
I said a moment ago.
The hon. member's time has expired.
The hon. member's time has expired.

Would the hon. member permit a question? This is the third time I have heard him speak in this parliament, and on each time he took about thirty-five minutes of his forty minutes quoting from Hansard or some pamphlet. My question is: Will he tell us when he is going to make a speech of his own.
