There is an actual price on soy beans.
I have not heard it announced, although I have been asking for it for a long time.

Not for this year; for
last year.
Mr. MacKENZIE (Lambton-Kent). It is the 1944 crop I am speaking of. They say that the Saskatchewan election was lost because of federal policy. When I was younger I believed in Santa Clause. As I got older I became disillusioned, but I am again reaching the place where I believe there is still a Santa Claus. If the Minister of Agriculture is not a Santa Claus to the western farmer then I do not believe they have ever seen one. He has gone down all their chimneys and I do not think they were big enough. They had to enlarge them so that he could go down again.
I think the price of Ontario wheat is too low. It should be raised to a ceiling price of $1.50 a bushel. I do not object to the western farmer getting a good price for his wheat and other crops, but I think the federation of agriculture is doing something to try to place agriculture on a higher plane. We must get agriculture in the position where it will get its fair share of the national income. The east and west should get together to support the federation of agriculture. I do not care whether you call it a farm bloc or something else, but the fact remains that these people are interested in agriculture being placed on a sound economic basis so that it can get its fair share of the national income.
[Mr. H. A. MacKemie.l
If we are going to retain the young people on the farm; if we are going to retain people in the rural districts, we must take some of the drudgery out of farm life; we must make farm life more livable. Many times in this house I have heard it told of how farmers years ago had to sleep on straw ticks or on corn husks. I have done all those things. I have lived in a shack without modern conveniences. That did not do me any harm, but I do not think we should expect our young people to do it to-day. As a matter of fact they will not do it. There are thousands of young people who have gone to the factories in Detroit and Windsor and Sarnia because living conditions and income were not right at home.
One thing that should be emphasized is the increased need for hydro power and electricity. An hon. member from Manitoba the other night gave percentages of farms with hydro power. I believe he claimed that in Ontario forty per cent of the farms had electricity, but the last report I had showed only thirty-one per cent. However, I believe a lot of hydro power has been put in during the last year.
I saw a press dispatch the other day to the effect that daylight saving was working out very well and would be retained after the war, and I believe it stated that the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) had said that the demand for hydro power would increase if we went back to standard time. I am not so sure about that, because most industries are working twenty-four hours a day and the lights are turned on when daylight ceases. I would not for the world want to deprive workers in factories of a long afternoon, but I do not see why they cannot start to work an hour earlier and leave the clock alone. I think the time will come when they will do that. You cannot save daylight; it just cannot be done. There was only one man who could ever save daylight, and that was Joshua when he made the sun stand still. We have no Joshuas in modern life to-day.
I just leave these few thoughts with you and I hope that we can organize in order to get rural life back into its proper place.

Mr. Speaker, were I to declare that the members of the Social Credit group have made a conscientious attempt to cooperate in shortening this debate I doubt if any would disagree. However, cooperation does not apply just to one group. For my part I have remained out of the house at least during parts of recent days so that I would not be aggravated into speaking. Unfortunately I came in to-night.
I have heard one speech which in itself could

The Budget-Mr. Shaw
be responsible for my participating at this time. I regret very much that I happen to be the one who appears to be carrying the debate over to another day.
I wish to say a number of things with respect to the remarks of the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank). It is regrettable that some people have such poor memories and do not take the time to go back and read the records once in a while. If they did that they would probably secure a proper understanding of the position which this and other groups took at the beginning of the present war. Before dealing further with this matter,
I should like to make a brief reference to the budget itself.
I think it is proper to say that the budget was more or less bereft of surprises. I know a great many people expected that there would be certain changes, the purpose of which would be to alleviate the burden of taxation probably to a great extent. As far as I am concerned I was not a bit surprised because I knew that if taxation had been lowered materially then borrowing, which is nothing but a deferred system of taxation, would have had to be increased. That is the penalty you pay when the method of financing the war is based on a policy of debt and taxation.
I know that many of those who believed there would be substantial reduction in taxation overlooked the fact that the cost of the war has not been lessened. We are going to be extremely fortunate if taxation remains where it is for the duration of the war, if our financial costs are not considerably greater than those we have encountered up to the present time.
More than that, as I said during a previous speech, I am not going to be astonished if taxation is not reduced after the war is over, because it has been said time and time again in this house that we have, alongside the very heavy taxation, built up municipal, provincial and federal debts of approximately $16,000 million. I sometimes wonder what the minister meant when during the early months of the war he indicated that we would pay for the war as it is being fought. In the destruction of material things and of human life we have paid a pretty costly price. When we take into consideration Prime Minister Churchill's assertion that the price is "blood, sweat and tears", it does make one feel badly to think that when the war is over we are going to start paying for it in a dollar and cent fashion. To confirm that statement all one has to do is recognize the extent of the national debt and its growth during the prosecution of the war. Another regrettable feature is that, of those boys who are fighting
overseas, apart from those who will never come back, the numbers who return maimed and the many, we hope, who will come back uninjured will themselves have to play a major part in financing the dollar cost of the war which they won-all, I assert, because the government persist in pursuing strictly orthodox methods of financing and are determined not to endeavour to alleviate at least the debt aspect of our war cost by utilizing national credit.
Another serious situation which has developed as a consequence of our present method of financing is that, in order to carry on, we have had to centralize more and more all activities. More than that, due at least in part to our method of financing, we have had to adopt more and more regimentation, much more than would have been necessary if we had adopted a democratic system of financing, at least in part.
Of course the method of financing has played no small part in the further restriction of certain liberties. I am not one who asserts that you can fight a war while continuing to live as usual. I am not one who would say that the government should not and must not and need not take unto itself certain authorities which in peace time we would deny it. I do not wish to be charged with suggesting that we should pursue life in the normal fashion. But as a result of the need of the government to centralize further, to regiment further, to restrict liberties further, there has developed among a cross-section of our people a respect for the principle of . totalitarianism. Probably I should make that clear. Unfortunately there are some who think that the success in connection with the war effort has been due largely to the fact that we have regimented, that we have deprived the people of liberties and so forth, and they have as I say developed some sort of strange love of this principle of regimentation. I find that largely true among a crosssection of people who have the tendency to encourage leadership rather than apply personal initiative. Our method of financing has been largely responsible for the growth of certain of these conditions.
I desire to make some remarks in reply to the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank), but since it is almost eleven o'clock I would prefer to do so upon an occasion when he is likely to be present.
On motion of Mr. Shaw the debate was adjourned.
